A tree was blown down in Lakeville, Minnesota.
A few 4 to 6 inch diameter trees were blown down near Vasa, Minnesota.
A large tree was uprooted near South Park and Forest in Fairmont, Minnesota.
A brief tornado moved across open fields and into Freeborn County. Tornado was recorded on video.

A brief tornado moved across open fields and groves of trees after developing in Faribault County. It snapped numerous power poles approximately five feet off the ground along County Road 11. Several dozen trees also had large branches snapped off. Tornado was photographed and recorded on video by chasers.
A metal shed building was blown in, with debris from the building up to a quarter mile away. Multiple trees were uprooted. The tornado was recorded on video by storm chasers.
The tornado broke several dozen trees. It was recorded on video by storm chasers.
This was a satellite tornado to the Conger EF-4. It damaged trees, several grain bins and structures.

Touchdown was near the intersection of Freeborn County Roads 14 and 20. Multiple farmsteads experienced significant structural and tree damage, including one house completely destroyed and several others heavily damaged.  Many outbuildings were  destroyed, hundreds of trees uprooted and snapped, with some partially debarked.  It then moved into Steele County, southwest of Ellendale, where it began moving to the north-northwest.

This tornado moved from Freeborn County and into Steele County and began moving to the north-northwest, thereby missing the city of Ellendale. At about (43.9255, -93.3453), it began moving toward the northwest, and at about (43.9407, -93.3627), it actually turned some more and moved toward the west-northwest until it finally dissipated.  Accounting for the change in direction, the tornado had an actual path length of 7.7 miles in Steele County.  Along the way, several homes experienced significant structural damage, with one house completely destroyed and the roof removed from two others.  Many outbuildings were destroyed, and hundreds of trees were uprooted and snapped.

This tornado touched down near the intersection of Interstate 35 and Freeborn County Road 31.  Multiple outbuildings were destroyed and numerous large trees were broken or toppled.  It exited Freeborn County just north of Geneva, where it continued into Steele County.

This tornado originated in Freeborn County, near Clark's Grove and producing minor damage in Geneva. It entered Steele County near County Road 45 and 168th Street SW and moved north-northeast for most of the time it existed, but at about (43.9154, -93.2159), it turned and began moving to the north-northwest, and dissipated while on its north-northwest track. Thus, the overall path length was 12.93 miles when accounting for the change in direction.  In Steele County, several outbuildings were destroyed, the roof was taken off a barn, and numerous large trees were downed.

A tornado developed just to the southeast of the intersection of County Roads 30 and 35, or about 1/4 mile southeast of where the Hollandale EF-3 had dissipated. This new tornado tracked northeast, hitting three farmsteads just east of the intersection of county roads 30 and 35.  Numerous trees were snapped and a shed and other outbuildings were destroyed. For the latter portion of its track, the tornado moved through fields and groves, with more crop damage and broken trees.  Photos and video recorded by storm chaser.

This tornado developed just north of the Steele/Freeborn County line, shortly after the dissipation in Freeborn County of the Newry tornado.  This new tornado moved northeast, and initially, occasional trees were broken. Damage intensified somewhat when it hit a farm on State Highway 30 just west of Blooming Prairie. The tornado continued moving northeast, decimating crops. Some bean fields were scoured in spots.  It intensified significantly to EF-3 2.5 miles northwest of Blooming Prairie, where a house was leveled, trees were snapped, and large portions of bark were removed. A pickup truck was lofted about 50 feet into the basement of the house.  Several other houses sustained minor damage.  The tornado dissipated just west of Highway 218 and 123rd Street.  Video recorded by law enforcement and chasers.

This tornado moved north-northeast and caused minor damage to outbuildings and broke several dozen trees.  It exited Steele County about 3/4 mile south of Steele County Road 26 and continued into Dodge County.

This EF-2 tornado touched down and tracked east-northeast, and soon crossed the path of the Blooming Prairie EF-3 that had moved north-northeast about 10 minutes earlier.  A manufactured home was obliterated by the EF-2.  A woman inside the home was blown about 20 feet, but was found under debris, rescued by law enforcement, and survived.  The tornado continued moving east-northeast, and several outbuildings were destroyed, along with many broken trees. The tornado continued into Dodge County.
The tornado touched down in a rural area.  Some trees were broken, a gravity box was tipped over, and minor crop damage occurred.

Isolated tree damage was noted near the initial touchdown location, but the damage became more concentrated and more intense as the storm approached Constance Lake. Low end EF-1 tornado damage was noted, as the trunks of several trees were snapped at locations on both sides of the lake. An intermittent damage path continued further north, with damage to trees and a small lean-to shelter. The tornado dissipated near the intersection of 85th St NE and Cahill Ave.
About two dozen trees were broken, windows were blown out at one house, a flag pole was bent, and minor damage to some sheds was noted.
Numerous trees were broken or snapped, producing EF-1 damage in Douglas County, then the tornado continued into Otter Tail County, where it intensified to EF-4.

A tornado touched down in extreme northern Chisago County, uprooting trees and breaking large branches. It then moved into Pine County, where it intensified and produced EF-2 damage, and eventually tracked into Burnett County, Wisconsin.

This tornado destroyed a barn, broke dozens of trees, and damaged a few sheds.  As it began to dissipate, it became very narrow and then rotated halfway around a new tornado west of Hollandale.  Video filmed by storm chaser.

Significant street flooding occurred in St. James, Minnesota where several low areas were impassable. A Minnesota Department of Transportation Weather Station near Madelia, Minnesota estimated 4.90 inches of rainfall between 7:30 PM to 9:30 PM CST.
Several spotters across the southern part of Mankato, Minnesota reported water covering roadways due to excessive rainfall.
Several large trees were uprooted and blocking the intersections of Warren and Highland near Mankato, Minnesota.
A tornado tore through a wooded area, knocking down or shearing off a couple hundred trees.

A tornado moved southeast across mostly open fields, causing only minor damage at a couple of farmsteads. About 1/2 mile southeast of Highway 14 and Garden Avenue, however, it struck a farmstead, demolishing two sheds, and peeling away a portion of a barn roof. The house sustained minor damage, and the tornado uprooted or broke several dozen trees. The tornado then turned south-southeast and hit one more farmstead, knocking down more trees and causing minor damage to a house. The tornado was recorded on video by storm chasers.
About a dozen trees were broken or snapped, and shingles were taken off the roof of a barn. Viewed by multiple eyewitnesses.
Spotter watched tornado move from north to south along 750th Avenue. Corn was damaged, along with a few trees and large branches. Multiple eyewitnesses.

Several dozen trees were broken or snapped. The top of the elevator was sheared off. Several sheds were destroyed. This was the last tornado from a complex that moved southeast and which produced a series of tornadoes that began around Courtland of Nicollet County.
This tornado damaged several farmsteads. A barn was caved in on a side, roofs of hog barns were blown off, trees were snapped or uprooted, and a wood pole was snapped.

The tornado touched down on the west side of Courtland, near Highway 14. The tornado produced EF-1 damage in the town of Courtland, where numerous trees were uprooted and many large tree branches were downed. The tornado continued east- southeast and strengthened in intensity just south of County Highway 25, where it produced EF-2 damage to multiple farmsteads. Damage included total destruction of a barn just west of the intersection of 511th avenue and County Highway 25. Widespread tree damage and snapped electrical transmission lines were also noted.

Two farmsteads were hit near the intersection of 260th Street and County Road 10, with one receiving considerable damage.  A barn was 2/3 destroyed, a harvestore silo was dented in about 70 feet off the ground, a corn crib was flattened, multiple wagons were displaced approximately 50 yards, and a wooden pole rated to 118 mph was cracked at the base.
A funnel cloud was reported near County Road 22, and County Road 1.
Winds were estimated around 45 mph, along with dime size hail and 1.18 inches of rainfall.
Several trees and power lines were blown down north of Brandon, Minnesota.
A large tree was uprooted near St. Joseph, Minnesota.

Severe straight-line winds caused a patio awning to blow away, a port-a-potty to blow over, and several 2-3 inch diameter tree limbs to be torn off a large tree. In addition, the northern portion of Milaca, Minnesota, lost power.
A Minnesota Department of Transportion Weather Sensor, measured a wind gust of 51 knots near Lastrup, Minnesota.
Several trees were blown down near the intersection of Interstate 494 & 694.
An 8 inch diameter tree was blown down near Bayport, Minnesota.
A local trained spotter measured a 54 knot wind gust near Afton, Minnesota.
An 18 inch diameter tree was blown down near River Falls, Wisconsin. In addtion, another trained spotter reported a funnel cloud west of River Falls.
Barn walls collapsed and a garage was pushed off its foundation. Power poles were snapped and multiple trees uprooted.
The tornado produced widespread damage to campers, roofs, docks, and sheds. Numerous trees were broken or uprooted.
The tornado struck several groves of trees, snapping some near the base. It also ripped the top of a silo, spreading tin into an adjacent field. A garage door was also pushed inward.
Several dozen trees were broken, garage doors were dented in, and damage was done to siding, soffits, and shingles on numerous houses.
A brief tornado destroyed a chicken coop, partially took the roof off a shed, and broke several trees.
Numerous trees were broken, mostly in a cemetery on the west edge of Wells.
Several trees were broken, the roof was partially removed from a large shed, a grain bin was damaged, outbuildings sustained minor damage, and a narrow path was observed in an adjacent corn field.
Dozens of trees were broken or uprooted, two grain bins were destroyed, an auger was moved, several sheds were damaged, and a granary was moved.
Numerous trees were knocked down associated with the rear flank downdraft that accompanied the tornado that entered Steele County at 1833 LST.
Numerous trees were knocked down associated with the rear flank downdraft that accompanied the tornado that originated just east of Clark's Grove at 1815 LST.
Dozens of trees were broken or uprooted and several sheds were destroyed due to rear flank downdraft winds that accompanied the Hollandale EF-3 tornado.
A strong rear flank downdraft accompanied the Wells tornado.  The winds knocked down numerous trees, mostly in the south side of the city of Wells.
A funnel had been visible for several minutes before it touched down.  The tornado stirred up some dirt, knocked over some small items, and tore off a few shingles.
Several large trees were blown down from near Clements, to one mile north of Clements, including one tree that fell on a car.
Numerous large 12-18 inch diameter trees were blown down along Highway 25 and near the intersection of Highway 25, and 158th Street. Also, a few power lines were knocked down due to the trees.
A few power lines were blown down due to severe straight-line winds.
A large tree limb was blown down, and fell on a truck near 225th Street, and Chippendale Avenue.
A trained spotter measured a 59 knot wind gust at the intersection of Highway 8 and 14.

Six inches of flowing water occurred at the intersection of County Road C2 and Marion Street. Rainfall reports from several observers in Ramsey County had between three and five inches between 8 and 11 pm. One observer reported 4 inches of rainfall in less than two hours.

County Road 50 was covered with six inches of water at one point east of Pilot Knob Road, near Farmington, Minnesota. In addition, 9 inches of water was reported along Chippendale Ave West, near Ash St, and Elm St.  1 to 2 feet of water was reported in fields south of 225th St. West. A few buses and police cars were stuck in water near Central Ave and 20th Street, north of downtown Minneapolis, Minnesota. Several observers across Hennepin County, especially near the downtown area, had between two and locally five inches  of rainfall between 8 and 11 pm.
Several 4 to 6 inch diameter tree limbs were blown down in Cornell, Wisconsin.
Numerous cars were stalled across the city of River Falls, Wisconsin due to rainfall amounts of three to five inches in less than 4 hours.
Several cars had stalled due to excessive water on roadways in Prescott, Wisconsin.
Local officials reported six inches of running water over several roads in Spring Valley, Wisconsin.
Significant street flooding was reported in Cornell, Wisconsin where storm sewers were overflowing. Overnight rainfall reports were averaging between three and five inches across the county.

Significant flooding was observed across much of the northern half of Dunn County. Roads were washed out in Colfax Township, south of Colfax. More roads were washed out in Lucas Township. Several observers reported between three and six inches of rainfall overnight across the county.
Major street flooding was reported on Hastings Way, and Valmont Avenue in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, which was observed to have over 8 inches of water across the road.

Significant flood waters were washing over several roads in Woodville, Wisconsin. Some residents in town had flood waters in their home. A few observers reported rainfall totals overnight around six inches.
An apartment building and nursing home was evacuated due to flood waters. The southeast portion of Baldwin was hardest hit. A concrete bridge was washed out in town, along with 15 feet of roadway.
An observer in Clayton, Wisconsin, reported basement flooding with approxmately two inches of water covering the floor.
Significant street flooding was reported in Faribault, Minnesota.  Water was up to two foot in some locations, and covering major intersections.
Very heavy rainfall, and the associated street flooding, caused numerous cars to be stranded across city streets from Burnsville to Lakeville, Minnesota.
Several streets in Prior Lake had major street flooding due to rainfall rates as high as two inches per hour.  It caused several cars to stall on Eagle Creek Road, and Grainwood Road.
Significant street flooding was reported in the south side of Owatonna, Minnesota.
Several retaining walls collapsed due to excessive rainfall amounts, and caused mud flows and logs to flow onto city streets.
Flood waters were high enough to strand several cars east of Old Shakopee Road and France Avenue in Bloomington, Minnesota..
Rainfall rates were so high, that several manhole covers were blown off in Red Wing, Minnesota.

Several trees were blown down near Cleveland, Minnesota.

A Storm Survey determined that an EF-1 tornado tracked to the northeast from three miles northwest of Farmington, to 3.3 miles north of Farmington, Minnesota. ||The damage consisted of the following; ||A few homes had large sections of roof structure removed. Numerous homes had significant roof damage, with loss of vinyl or metal siding. In addtion, numerous garage doors had collapsed or were pushed inward. One home had their entire garage shifted off its foundation by over 5 inches. Another home had their entire garage collapse, only leaving the main home intact. Due to several structures that had their foundations shifted and walls completely blown down, this tornado was rated a high end EF-1, which is approximately 105 mph. Downburst damage was observed along a seven mile long path, oriented from northwest to southeast, in northwestern Polk County. The maximum width of the damage area was about 400 yards.  The most intense damage consisted of numerous large trees being snapped and uprooted, with substantial branch loss on the north side of Little Mirror Lake to near the intersection of County Road N and 195th St. A few trees fell on garages and homes. One barn was heavily damaged. Silo roofs were blown off.
Several trees were blown down in the Georgetown area.
Numerous large pine trees were toppled.

A tornado traveled from west to east across the northern edge of the village of Balsam Lake.  A small grove of large trees was completely uprooted just north of downtown Balsam Lake.  There were 2 garages which has all sides blown in. Other large trees were snapped or uprooted, with a few ending up on houses. A shed was blown over.

A tornado traveled east-southeast, just north of the village of Turtle Lake.  It touched down in extreme eastern Polk County and moved into Barron County.  In Polk County, a large outbuilding was completely destroyed 1.5 miles north-northwest of Turtle Lake, with debris scattered downstream for hundreds of yards. Scattered large trees were snapped or uprooted.

A tornado traveled east-southeast, just north of the village of Turtle Lake.  It touched down in extreme eastern Polk County and moved into Barron County.  In Barron County, roofs were peeled off on a few homes.  Scattered large trees were snapped or uprooted. The tornado crossed Highway 63, and multiple downed trees resulted in the closure of Highway 63 for several hours.  It dissipated just before reaching Highway 8.
A large tree were downed across County Road SS.

A tornado in southeastern Barron County traveled southeast, touching down just southeast of Cameron and dissipating just north of Chetek.  Numerous very large trees were uprooted and snapped near the start of the path. There were over a dozen large pine trees down on the east shore of Prairie Lake, several of which fell on a home. A storage garage lost its roof and a turkey barn lost its roof.

A large area of downburst winds, with gusts of 90 mph, occurred north of Osseo, northward along County Road R, then northeast to around Augusta, Wisconsin, and  accompanied the two EF-1 tornadoes near Augusta. A farmstead just east of County Road R, and north of Osseo, was heavily damaged. In addition, several outbuildings were damaged, along with numerous power poles and trees snapped from the damaging downburst path that was estimated between 10 to 12 miles long. Some homes had minor damage to shingles.

An EF-1 tornado, with maximum wind speeds of 95 to 105 mph occurred from approximately 5 miles southwest of Augusta, to 3.5 miles southwest of Augusta, Wisconsin. Two farmsteads were directly impacted with severe tree damage around the homes. One farmstead had their garage completely destroyed along with a barn heavily damaged.

An EF-1 tornado, with maximum wind speeds of 90 to 100 mph, occurred along a path from northwest of Augusta to north of Augusta, Wisconsin. Numerous trees and power poles were snapped, along with an outbuilding destroyed, and three other outbuildings significantly damaged.
This was measured by the Fire Weather RAWS site.

Some of the major routes included 169, 22, and 93 and 99.  There was one fatality on March 22 when a MNDOT worker tried to clear an ice jam and his Backhoe tipped over and fell into the area where Seven Mile Creek flows into the Minnesota River.

Several county roads and highways were closed due to Spring melting along the Minnesota River, and some of its tributaries from Milan, to Montevideo to around Granite Falls, Minnesota. One of the major routes that was closed partially was Highway 7.

Several highways and county roads were closed due to Spring snow melt and associated flooding along the Minnesota and Yellow Medicine Rivers. Some of the main roads that were closed due to the flooding were Highways 59 and 23.

One home lost part of its roof, and others lost shingles. Several homes had windows blown in. Several dozen trees and a number of power poles were broken or knocked down. Siding and soffits were ripped off a few houses. Numerous backyard fences were blown over. A pole barn was lifted up about three feet before being set back down.  The tornado was photographed and videotaped by several people. The condensation funnel was not fully extended, and the debris cloud never extended as high as the condensation funnel. The tornado was a marginal EF-1, with winds near 90 mph.

One eight inch diameter pine tree, plus several large limbs were blown down due to strong post-thunderstorm winds. This occurred around the Sand Creek area. Time is approximate due to strong winds for several hours.

Several large pine trees, up to 24 inches in diameter, were blown down in the wake of a large thunderstorm complex that moved across the area during the late morning.  This occurred in the Rice Lake, Wisconsin area. Time is approximate due to strong winds for several hours.

Several large white pines, up to 70 feet high, were blown down due to strong winds in the wake of a thunderstorm complex that moved across the area. This occurred around the Eau Claire, Wisconsin area. Time is approximate due to strong winds for several hours.

An EF-0 tornado briefly touched down near 155th Street Northeast, and County Highway 17 east of Ham Lake.  Damage was confined to trees blown down and a few shingles ripped off homes.

A strong EF-1 tornado touched down approximately 3/4 of a mile south-southwest of the intersection of Interstate 394 and Highway 100 in St. Louis Park, Minnesota. It traveled north-northeast through Golden Valley, and across North Minneapolis, before moving into Anoka County. ||Damage was widespread along the path and caused damage to businesses near the intersection of Interstate 394, and Highway 100.  As it crossed Highway 100, it began to damage numerous residences along Cedar Lake Road before moving into Theodore Wirth Park.  The tornado moved across Wirth Park, and into the City of North Minneapolis, between Glenwood Avenue and 16th Avenue. ||Most of the damage at this point was EF-0 and was confined to downed trees and roof damage.  It strengthened to EF-1 as it moved into North Minneapolis.  The tornado tracked across Penn Avenue and Broadway, then to Lowry Avenue and Logan Avenue, then to 42nd Avenue to Lyndale Avenue before crossing the Mississippi River.  Damage along this path was extensive to garages, with sheds and roofs removed.||A male was killed as a tree fell on his car while he was driving in North Minneapolis. City officials stated that more than 600 buildings would require major repairs, and 35 homes were so badly damaged they could not be reoccupied.

An EF-1 tornado continued into Anoka County from the Camden Bridge along the Mississippi River, north-northeast to the east side of Fridley, to Spring Lake where it moved into Ramsey County. ||Damage was extensive along the path where it moved into a rail yard and a large industrial facility. A large metal building roof was ripped off in the industrial area, and eight train cars were tipped over where EF-1 damage was observed. Several warehouses sustained damaged along Miami Street where a roof was blown off. ||The tornado then moved across residential sections of Fridley, before it weakened as it continued northeast across the east side of Fridley, near Spring Lake. Damage was confined to trees blown down along the path, then moved into Ramsey County.

An EF-0 tornado continued in Ramsey County, near Spring Lake, then north-northeast as it crossed back into Anoka County, near Highway 10, south of the Blaine-Anoka County Airport. Most of the damage was confined to sporadic trees blown down along the path.

An EF-0 continued into Anoka County, and dissipated on the south side of the Blaine-Anoka County Airport.  Damage was confined to several hangers on the airport grounds, that had their exterior walls damaged.

An EF-0 tornado touched down near 200th Street and Imperial Avenue, or about three miles southeast of Forest Lake, Minnesota. It moved north-northeast, and dissipated on the north side of Forest Lake, near Shadeland Point.  Damaged was confined to trees, roof shingles, and a large metal shed.  The tornado was viewed by multiple spotters, chasers, law enforcement officers, and was seen on a MNDOT camera.

An EF-1 tornado touched down just west of the intersection of 28th Avenue and 26th Street. It tracked northeast and dissipated at 30th Avenue. Damage was sporadic along this tornado path, with damages to roofs, a 12 foot house antenna, two seven foot tall horse enclosures, and numerous large trees uprooted and blown down.

An EF-0 tornado touched down just south of Elysian Lake Road, just south of 412th Avenue, in northern Waseca County. The tornado tracked north for approximately 2.8 miles while paralleling the eastern shore of Elysian Lake and Elysian Lake Road. It crossed Elysian Lake near 427th Ave, before moving into southern Le Sueur County. ||Damage was primarily associated with uprooted trees and roof damage. The worst damage occurred to a farmstead which had a metal storage shed collapse along Elysian Lake Road. ||Based on trees uprooted and structural damage to a metal storage shed, winds were estimated around 80 mph.

The EF-0 tornado that formed in northern Waseca County continued to move northward across the western sections of Elysian in Le Sueur County, where two small empty grain bins were blown into a field. Also, a small metal shed was blown across Highway 60 in the same area. ||As the tornado continued to track north of Lake Francis, the damage pattern became more complex, and some damage signatures were associated with downburst winds. However, the damage pattern was such that it impossible to discern between the tornado damage and any downburst damage.  Therefore there is no separate entry for thunderstorm wind damage at this point.  ||The path length of the tornado in Le Sueur County was approximately 3.7 miles, which ended at the St. Peters Church two miles north of Lake Francis. Although most of the damage was associated with uprooted trees and roof damage to homes, numerous boat docks and lifts along the northern shore of Lake Francis were picked up and tossed into the adjacent properties.  ||Based on damage, winds were estimated at 80 mph, and the total path length across Waseca and Le Sueur Counties was 6.54 miles.

Several witnesses and storm spotters observed a tornado touchdown south of Lucan, Minnesota.  The tornado tracked to the southeast and damaged a farmhouse, which included several outbuildings, a greenhouse, pole barn, and shed.  Based on damage the tornado was rated an EF0 with top winds of 80 mph.  The tornado lifted one quarter of a mile southeast of the farmhouse where debris was thrown one half mile.

Based on damage from a barn and grainery, the tornado was rated an EF0 with wind speeds of 75 mph.

Local law enforcement officials confirmed that a tornado briefly touched down northeast of Farwell, Minnesota.  Based on damage of a 30-40 foot pole barn, and minor damage to a second barn, the tornado was rated an EF0 with top winds of 75 mph.

A tornado touchdown briefly approximately 3 miles northwest of Chokio, Minnesota.  The report is based on a storm chaser's photo. No damage occurred and the tornado lifted quickly.

Heavy rainfall occurred during the early evening of May 2nd. Flooding was observed in the town of Warsaw, with flood waters up to 5 feet in residential areas, stalled cars, and several roads impassable.

Heavy rainfall fell during the evening of May 2nd. Flooding was observed in the town of Faribault, especially in the southeast part of town where flood waters rose up to 5 feet in some residential areas. Heavy rainfall across Goodhue County caused flooding on Highway 57, along the North Fork of the Zumbro River, north of Wanamingo, Minnesota.  In addition, over two inches of rainfall was measured near Wanamingo.
Several large tree branches and one large tree blew down in the southern part of Litchfield. In addition, a plane was flipped over at the Litchfield airport.

A weak tornado touched down and moved northeast for a little more than one mile to 44.81784W, 93.97340N.  It then turned slightly and moved east-northeast until dissipation.  Corn and several dozen trees were damaged as the tornado mostly moved over fields.  An old barn along County Road 33 was blown down, killing 12 cows.
A funnel cloud was reported northwest of Cumberland. There were no reports of touchdowns.

The Barron County Medical Examiner found that a 71 year old woman died from heat in her apartment.  The wall thermometer read 105 degrees. The family stated that she refused to have an air conditioner, stating she did not like the cold.  In addition, the Barron County Medical Examiner determined that a 76 year old woman died of heat on July 1st. The county official reported that she was in a motorized wheelchair that left the roadway and went into a ditch. She was unable to get back onto the dead-end road and was found approximately 6-7 hours later. The temperature during that time frame was 86 to 89 degrees. She suffered from multiple sclerosis and was too weak to get out of the ditch. The deceased was found sitting in her wheelchair.
A large tree was blown down near Stanley.
A large tree fell on a house in Albert Lea.  In addition, there were reports of widespread tree damage across parts of Freeborn County, along with power outages.
A private weather station measured a wind gust of 58 mph.
A few trees were blown down in Wells, Minnesota. Power outages also occurred.
A Minnesota Department of Transportation weather sensor, along Interstate 90,  measured a wind gust of 58 mph.

A lightning strike triggered a fire that significantly damaged a home in Maple Grove, Minnesota. Residents of the home at 18868 63rd Place awoke to the sound of a lightning strike, smelled smoke and called 911. The residents were not hurt, but damage to the roof and upper floor of the home was described as significant. There was also water and smoke damage.

A brief EF-0 tornado developed east of Lilydale, just southeast of the intersection of Highway 13 and Wachtler Avenue.  It tracked northeast across a subdivision in extreme northern Mendota Heights. Several dozen large trees were blown down onto homes, cars and sheds.
A few trees were blown down from Mounds Park, then north-northeast to around Johnson Parkway, and Minnehaha Avenue, then northeast to the White Bear Lake area.

This is a continuation in Ramsey County of the wind damage that hit Mendota Heights and West St. Paul in Dakota County.  It tracked northeast across south central St Paul, from Smith and Annapolis to St Paul Holman Field, but damage was more sporadic than when it hit Dakota County. Most of the damage was due to trees landing on cars, houses and sheds.

There were isolated trees, large branches and power lines down from the northeastern corner of Grant into the southern part of May Township near Big Carnelian Lake (about six miles north of Stillwater).  The wind also peeled heavy gauge steel off of a barn roof and took the large doors off.  The south end up of a farm shop was lifted up a few inches, pushing the west wall out and displacing the roof.  Power poles were down as well.
Measured at St Paul Holman Field.

An EF-0 tornado developed northeast of the intersection of County Road 5 and McAndrews Road, and tracked northeast to just southwest of the intersection of Burnsville Parkway and County Road 11. A large area of uprooted trees and power lines occurred along a non-continuous broken path of 2.8 miles in a heavily populated region of Burnsville. The worst damage occurred in a two block area between Knoll Lane and Nicollet Avenue, and Nicollet Jr High School.

A brief EF-0 tornado spun up near Skyline Drive, east of Highway 13, and tracked north-northeast to the Lost Spur Golf Course just south of Interstate 494. The tornado tracked for two blocks in a heavily wooded residential area before moving across a small golf course as it dissipated. Numerous large trees and power lines were blown down along the path of approximately one-half mile.

About two dozen trees were downed from Mendota to Lilydale, for about two miles along Highway 13, and on either side of Interstate 35E.  The trees were all oriented from southwest to northeast, and there was no concentrated area of damage. The damage was most likely due to rear flank downdraft winds.

A storm survey revealed that straight line winds of 65 mph were associated with the rear flank downdraft from the tornado that dissipated at the Lost Spur Golf Course. These severe winds blew shingles off a hotel roof and knocked down trees from near Interstate 494 and Pilot Knob Road, northeast to a business community.

A storm survey indicated a large downburst damage swath with numerous downed trees in the northeastern section of Mendota Heights, and the northern portion of West St. Paul. A large part of the damage pattern across northeastern Mendota Heights and West St. Paul was directed toward the east, northeast and north. It was a very standard pattern of downburst winds. Many of the trees landed on homes, cars and garages. Some of the garages were pushed off their foundations. Some of the most significant downburst damage was in a 5-10 block area surrounding Dodd Road, Delaware and Smith Avenue.

Hundreds of trees were toppled or snapped. Some trees fell on cars, houses and sheds.  The tornado touched down in Mahtomedi, just east of the White Bear Lake shore, and it moved northeast into the northeastern part of Grant.  The most significant damage was shortly after touchdown, near the intersection of Hazel and Moccasin in far northern Mahtomedi, where strong EF-0 damage was noted.

Several trees were knocked down or broken along the eastern shore of White Bear Lake.  This was most likely from a rear flank downdraft, and was associated with the storm that would soon produce the tornado in Washington County at 2321 CST.
Roof and siding damage occurred at a home in New Prague.

The Hennepin County Medical Examiner had three heat related deaths due to the prolonged heat wave in early July. One was a 78 year old individual who was likely working outdoors.  He was admitted to the hospital on the 5th with heat stroke conditions, and died on the 12th.  Another man, 46 years old, died on the 5th in his home, and the third person was a 66 year old female who was last seen on the 3rd and found in her home on the 12th.  During the week of July 2nd through the 5th, afternoon heat indices averaged between 100 and 110 degrees, with overnight lows in the mid to upper 70s.

Several sources in Carver County compiled a summary of flood related damages and locations for the flood of June 2014. More than 30 local and county roads were closed due to flooding, including the communities of Chaska, Mayer, Hollywood, Camden, Dahlgren, Young America, Laketown and Watertown. ||The Spring Creek levee failed in Carver. It caused significant mud slides affecting five private properties. In Cologne, 3 private residents had basement flooding. In Victoria, 6-8 homes had flooded basements. In Waconia, 4 homes had flooded basements. ||There were numerous county parks closed and several area lakes had no wake zones due to high water levels. ||During the height of the flooding, all river crossings along the Minnesota River were closed.

Several sources in Scott County compiled a summary of flood related damages and locations for the flood of June 2014. There were multiple reports of road closures due to high water and debris. Sporadic power outages reported throughout the county due to the water and electrical equipment being underwater. Mudslides and flood waters cut off all access to the town of Blakeley. This included train tracks that impacted Union Pacific and Canadian Pacific rail operations. Highways 6, 41 and 101 were all closed from flood waters of the Minnesota River. The town of Louisville, north of Jordan and west of Prior Lake, had two homes surrounded by flood waters during the height of the flood. Highway 169 was the only access from Scott County during the height of the flooding. In addition, no wake zones were posted on area lakes due to high levels and several parks were closed. Due to high levels on Prior Lake, County Road 21 was closed near the downtown area. In addition, numerous homes along the lake started to sandbag due to rising lake levels. In Shakopee, three rides were shut down at Valleyfair because of floodwaters that spilled into the park and across its parking lots.

Several sources in Dakota County compiled a summary of flood related damages and locations for the flood of June 2014. The City of Mendota was evacuated due to a large mudslide that affected several homes. The Minnesota Department of Transportation closed one lane on Interstate 35 due to the Minnesota River flood waters.

Several sources in Hennepin County compiled a summary of flood related damages and locations for the flood of June 2014. In Minneapolis a 100-yard mudslide occurred at the edge of the Fairview-University of Minnesota Hospital. No structural damage occurred and engineers determined that there was no threat to the hospital. Debris from this mudslide did flow into the Mississippi River and caused problems downstream at the locks and dams. In Edina and St. Louis Park, flood waters approached Methodist Hospital due to the swollen Minnehaha Creek. Several streets along Minnehaha Creek were flooded from the headwaters near Woodland, downstream to the Mississippi River. Numerous homes and businesses along the Minnehaha Creek were sandbagged due to the potential of being flooded. In addition, area lakes had a no wake zone for boats due to very high lake levels. Local officials indicated that in the city of Edina, 48 homes had flood damage, both from creek and other flooding, as well as from sewer backups.||The record rainfall on Thursday, June 19 caused Lake Minnetonka���s water level to reach an all-time high of 930.77 feet above sea level, breaking the previous record of 930.66 feet set on June 3, 2014.||In addition to the high lake levels in Hennepin County, 40 homes in the city of Mound were uninhabitable due to flood-related sewage backups near Lake Minnetonka.

Several sources in Ramsey County compiled a summary of flood related damages and locations for the flood of June 2014.||Due to the flood waters affecting downtown St. Paul, and covering Harriet Island, the Taste of Minnesota and the 4th of July Fireworks were moved to a different location. A supercell thunderstorm developed west of St. Cloud in eastern Stearns County around 3:45 PM CST. The storm gradually became better organized as it entered Benton County. A classic hook echo formed as it crossed U.S. Highway 10 around 4:25 PM CST and began to produce a tornado at 4:47 PM CST 3 miles south southwest of Morrill. The tornado produced a narrow swath of mainly tree damage along its path east northeast, but some minor structural damage was also noted - such as a roof being torn off from a farm outbuilding. The tornado moved into Morrison County at 4:56 PM CST. The tornado was photographed and caught on video by numerous storm chasers, spotters and others.

A tornado continued to move into Morrison County from Benton County. This tornado produced mainly tree damage before lifting 4 miles west northwest of Rum|River at 5:02 PM CST. It was recorded on video by two completely independent experienced storm chasers. This tornado briefly touched down in an open field.  It was recorded on video by two completely independent experienced storm chasers. Times and locations of both chasers were checked very carefully, as radar only showed a weak echo west of Clontarf at the time of the tornado.
This tornado moved across an open field. It was photographed and recorded on video by two independent storm chasers and also viewed by multiple trained spotters.

A tornado produced damage at a farm. A 100' x 70' long machine shed was destroyed when it was pushed off its foundation, with metal blown 1.5 miles downwind. Much of the equipment inside the shed was destroyed. A metal fence was blown down, and dozens of trees were broken. The tornado even clipped off some of the new soybeans that had emerged and were only one or two inches out of the ground.
A tornado moved across open fields. It was recorded on video by numerous storm chasers.
This tornado was recorded on video by multiple storm chasers. It briefly touched down in an open field.

This tornado mostly moved across open fields, and was recorded on video by numerous storm chasers and spotters.  After it touched down in an open field east of Terrace, it lifted off briefly and came back down a couple of times before moving through the western edge of Sedan.  The tornado caused about a dozen trees to be uprooted at a cemetery on the northwest edge of Sedan.  This was a multiple vortex tornado.  It also appears there may have been a satellite tornado that touched down in the back yard of a house on County Road 29, 1/2 mile south of Sedan, but the video is inconclusive as to whether it was a satellite tornado or part of the main tornadic circulation.
A tornado touched down in an open field. It was recorded on video by numerous storm chasers.
The tornado touched down for brief times on several occasions before it dissipated.  It was recorded on video by multiple storm chasers.
The last tornado in a series touched down in an open field.  It was recorded on video by multiple storm chasers.

A downburst associated with a decaying funnel cloud hit several groves of trees. A trained spotter from the area provided a very detailed map and photos of the damage. The photos clearly showed the tree damage occurred in a divergent pattern.
A storm chaser recorded video of a funnel when it was over Minnesota.

Video from a storm chaser showed a funnel that was completely separate from the circulation that produced the Sedan tornado and the tornado 2 to 4 miles north of Sedan from 1841 to 1847.  It is possible this touched down, but there is not enough evidence to be certain.
Local officials determined that lightning started a fire, and also damaged a gas meter in Rice, Minnesota. The damage was limited mostly to the exterior of the house.
During the early morning hours of Monday, June 8th, lightning struck a home in Eau Claire, Wisconsin. It caused extensive damage, but no one was hurt.
The public reported several trees blown down near Cold Spring, Minnesota.
There were multiple large tree limbs blown down near Danvers, Minnesota.
Several trees were blown down southwest of Canby, Minnesota.
There were several reports of penny to quarter size hail from west of Richmond, to east of Richmond. The largest hail stone was 1.25 inches in diameter northwest of the city.
There were several reports of penny to nickel size hail between Cold Spring and Rockville. The largest hail stone was quarter size, near Cold Spring.
There were several reports of penny to nickel size hail from south of Clearwater, east to Interstate 94. The largest hail stone was quarter size, south of Clearwater.
There were several reports of penny to nickel size hail northwest of Big Lake, and through the north and northeast part of town. The largest hail stone was quarter size, northeast of Big Lake.

Local officials in Stearns County reported flooding southeast of Freeport on County Road 172 and 157 after midnight.  A few cars and a party bus floated off the road into a ditch at that location. One person was injured when the party bus tipped over in the ditch. Part of the road was damaged due to flood waters flowing over that roadway. The town of Albany also had street flooding.
Large trees and a wooden swing were blown down north of Waseca near County Road 13.
Several trees were blown down along I-35 near Ellendale.

Two to three inches of rain fell in a small area of north central Freeborn County near Clarks Grove. There was a picture from social media of a flooded park which had 2-3 feet of standing water, which affected a large part of the outdoor shelter and play area.
Numerous trees were blown down along with a roof blown off a commercial building near Vernon Center.
A tree was uprooted and fell onto a car and building causing significant damage in Sherburn.
A large tree was blown down and landed on a house in St. James.
A tree was blown down and landed on a house in Fairmont.
A tree was blown down in Albert Lea.
Trees were reported blown down north of Ellendale.
The town of Comfrey had 6-7 blocks of tree debris from severe straight line winds. Power was out for an hour around the community.
Crops were damaged due to severe straight line winds around Sleepy Eye. In addition, tree branches were blown down in the town of Sleepy Eye, which blocked part of Highway 4.
Two large trees and several large tree branches were blown down in the southwest part of Hanska. Crops were also damaged in parts of Lake Hanska Township. Power was out in Hanska for 4 hours.

The tornado mostly crossed corn and bean fields, but it did originate near a freshly cut alfalfa field. The alfalfa was easily blown and resulted in a debris signature on radar. The tornado produced very minor damage at a few farmsteads, and knocked down several dozen trees along with breaking many large branches. The tornado was also photographed by a local resident.
Large tree branches and power outages occurred in the town of Bellingham.
Several large tree branches were blown down in Dawson.
A measured wind gust of 56 knots occurred northwest of Boyd.

A swath of large hail, the largest being ping pong ball size, occurred in an area between the Lac Qui Parle, and Big Stone County line, southeast toward the town of Cerro Gordo.  The combination of hail and wind caused considerable damage to the row crops in this area as well as substantial building/property damage. It was also indicated that an estimated 10,600 acres of soybeans were likely destroyed and another 10,600 acres were damaged.

The local emergency manager received damage reports in areas east of Highway 75, and north of Highway 40 as a severe storm moved through. The following are some of the reports received: one hog barn destroyed, 13 power poles broken, 3 grain bins damaged, one hoop barn damaged, one machine shed damaged, one 5th wheel livestock trailer destroyed, numerous windows broken, and house siding damaged.
Several reports of large hail occurred north of Columbus, southwest to the east of Ham Lake. The largest hail stone was ping pong size.
Several reports of large hail occurred around the city of Blaine. The largest hail stone was ping pong size. Hail damage to cars also occurred in the Lowes parking lot in Blaine.
A trained spotter reported a funnel cloud east of Highway 169.
Numerous reports of large hail occurred for several minutes around the city of Otsego. The largest hail stone was golf ball size. The local emergency manager indicated some crop damage around Otsego.
Numerous reports of large hail occurred north, east and southeast of Rogers. The largest hail stone was quarter size.
Numerous reports of large hail occurred between Corcoran and Maple Grove, southeast toward Highway 55. The largest hail stone was two inches in diameter.
There were several reports of hail west and south of Elk River. The largest hail stone was nickel size.
Large branches were blown down near Dallas and Berkshire road.
Numerous reports of large hail occurred around Plymouth, west of Plymouth, then southward toward the intersection of Interstate 494, and 394. The largest hail stone was golf ball size.

Several reports of large hail occurred near in the intersection of Highway 62 and Interstate 494, southward around Eden Prairie Center and the junction of 494 and 169.  The largest hail stone was quarter size.
Several reports of hail occurred near the city of Prior Lake. The largest hail stone was ping pong size.
A tree was blown down in the Rush Lake area. Plus, sliding damage occurred due to the large hail and wind near Rush Lake.
Several reports of large hail occurred around Rush Lake, and Rush City. The largest hail stone was 3 inches in diameter.
Several reports of large hail occurred around the city of North Branch. The largest hail stone was tennis ball size.
Several reports of large hail occurred at and near Wyoming to Chisago City in southern Chisago County. The largest hail stone was quarter size.
Several reports of half dollar size hail around the town of Forest Lake.
Several reports of large hail occurred near Withrow, or north of Grant and east of Hugo. The largest hail stone was half dollar size.
Several reports of large hail occurred around the cities of Spring Lake Park, Fridley and Columbia Heights. The largest hail stone was ping pong size.
Several reports of large hail occurred near the intersection of Interstate 35 and 694. The largest hail stone was quarter size.
Several reports of large hail occurred northwest, west and southwest of the city of Plymouth. The largest hail stone was two inches in diameter.
Several reports of large hail occurred near the intersection of Interstate 494 and 394, south-southeast toward the city of Minnetonka. The largest hail stone was ping pong size.
Ping pong size hail was reported in the St. Paul, Highland Park area.
Several reports of large hail occurred in the city of Shakopee. The largest hail stone was quarter size.

Multiple vehicles were reported stuck in high water at the intersection of 33rd Avenue and 8th Street North in St. Cloud.  Other areas in the city of St. Cloud reported minor ponding of water at some intersections.

Rainfall totals exceeded 4-5 inches in a 3 hour period early Monday morning, July 6th.  A resident in Woodbury reported rising water approaching their home. Heavy rains overflowed a pond and the athletic area at Highlands Park in Cottage Grove.
A rainfall amount of 2.11 inches occurred in Milaca in less than an hour.
Power lines and a large tree were blown down in the eastern part of Milaca.
A two foot diameter tree was blown down in Milltown and landed on a house.
A local newspaper had several large trees blown down in Evansville.
A measured wind gust of 70 knots was reported by a trained spotter with a mobile anemometer.
Trees were blown down in St. Cloud.
A wind sensor at the Sauk Centre Airport measured a severe wind gust. A number of trees were blown down in Sauk Centre.
A wind sensor at the Mora Airport measured a severe wind gust.  Several trees were reported down in Mora.
A local Minnesota Department of Transportation RWIS wind sensor measured a severe wind gust.
Several trees were uprooted near Luck.
A few trees were blown down in Arland.
A few large, two foot diameter trees were blown down near Rice Lake.
A few trees were blown down near New Auburn.
Several trees were blown down near Albertville. A spotter measured a wind gust of 57 knots from his private mobile wind sensor.
Several large trees and power lines were blown down near Bertha.
Several trees and power lines were blown down along Highway 210 near and west of Hewitt.
Several trees and power lines were blown down near Clarissa.
Several trees and power lines were blown down near Browerville.
Large pine trees were uprooted along Interstate 94 south of Garfield.
Several large trees were blown down west of Garfield, along County Road 82.
Several large trees were uprooted in Brandon.
A large shed under construction was partially destroyed. The damage occurred on Halverson Road, south of County Road 82, east of Brandon.
A pontoon boat was thrown and flipped over on Maple Lake.

Downburst damage was noted north of the tornado track. Initially, wooden poles were leaning and several oak and pine trees were snapped, and this is where the strongest winds were noted. As the downburst entered Staples, dozens of large trees were uprooted and many large branches were broken from Airport Rd to the east side of town. Winds across Staples were estimated in the 60-70 mph range.
Power lines were blown down northeast of Garfield.
Several large trees were blown down south of Villard.
Large trees were uprooted in Villard.
A large tree limb was blown down in Kimball.
A traffic signal was damaged in St. Joseph.
A few trees were blown down in Albany.
A large tree was uprooted near Braham.
A large tree was blown down near Cambridge.
A few trees were blown down near North Branch.
A tree was blown across a road north of Dassel.
Three large trees blown down, with some crop damage on County Road 30 near Howard Lake.
A large tree was blown down in the southern part of French Lake Township.
A large tree was blown down in Shakopee.
A few large trees were blown down near Prior Lake.
A large tree blew down onto a power line on Riverview Drive in Monticello.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down in the far northwest portion of Morrison County.
A few trees were blown down in Amador Township, near Almelund.
Several trees and power lines were blown down in Rushseba Township, northeast of Rush City.
A few trees were blown down in the city of Onamia.
Several trees were toppled in Stanley along with power lines blown down. Portions of the city had no power for several hours. Several of the trees landed on homes and caused some damage to roofs.
Power lines were blown down east of Fall Creek.
Power lines were blown down southwest of Ludington.
Power lines were blown down in Augusta.
Power lines were blown down in Eau Claire.
A measured wind gust of 53 knots was reported by the Madison County Airport wind sensor.
A measured wind gust of 55 knots was reported by the Montevideo County Airport wind sensor.
A measured 50 knot wind gust was reported by the Granite Falls County Airport wind sensor.
A measured wind gust of 54 knots was reported by a trained spotter with a private weather station northwest of Boyd.
A measured wind gust of 53 knots was reported by the Benson County Airport wind sensor.
A measured wind gust of 59 knots was reported by a private weather station near Hamburg.
A measured wind gust of 50 knots was reported by a private weather station near Long Lake.
A measured wind gust of 53 knots was reported by a private weather station near Golden Valley.
A measured wind gust of 58 knots was reported by a private weather station near Edina.
A measured wind gust of 54 knots was reported by the St. Paul Airport ASOS sensor.
A measured wind gust of 61 knots was reported by a private mobile weather station near New Brighton. In addition, there were uprooted trees from New Brighton, northeast to Shoreview.
A large tree was blown down north of Weston.
A large tree was blown down near Spring Valley.
Several large trees were blown down in Eau Claire, causing roof damage to a few homes.
Several trees were blown down near Cleveland. The trees landed on homes, sheds and a car and caused substantial damage.
A one foot diameter tree was blown down east of New Richland.
A private weather station rain gauge measured 4.24 inches of rainfall near French Lake.
A private weather station rain gauge measured 3.95 inches of rainfall near Albert Lea.
Several trees and a fence were damaged north of Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin.
Trees and power lines were blown down in Chippewa Falls.
There were several reports of downed power lines and trees around the Chokio and Alberta area.

The local emergency manager reported wind damage, with large trees and tree limbs blown down throughout the county. A machine shed roof was damaged in Louisburg. Corn laid down and was damaged near Rosen. Power lines were blown down in Madison.
Large construction barricades were blown over in Montevideo.
A large tree limb was blown off and landed on a tent in the Swift Falls Campground. One individual was injured in the tent.
A large tree was toppled in Willmar.
A large tree fell on a power line in Brownton.

A large tree was blown down at Yacht Avenue and 100th Street northeast, north of Stewart. There were additional reports of wind gusts of 45 to 55 mph in Hutchinson as the squall line moved through northern McLeod County.
A roof was blown off a house on Vega Avenue, south of New Germany.
An amphitheater outer shell was ripped off. It occurred near downtown Mankato, and near the Minnesota River. Several large trees were toppled across town.
Several large trees and power lines were blown down in the city of Watertown.
A large tree was blown over in Montrose.
Several large tree branches were blown down southeast of Watertown on Nike Road.

A severe squall line that moved out of Carver County, and into Hennepin County produced significant tree, power pole and power line damage. Reports of numerous large trees were toppled or uprooted from the Hennepin, Carver County line, near Saint Bonifacius, to 4 miles northeast of Minnetrista, then east-northeast toward Maple Plain, Spring Lake and Orono. Numerous trees had diameters of over 12 inches. One of the hardest hit areas was near Saint Bonifacius, where a barn and silo were damaged. The Spirit of the Lakes Festival had several tents blown down, with lots of reports of wires and sparking.

A severe squall line that moved from east to northeast across northern Carver County produced a significant swath of tree and power line damage across the city of Waconia. Several of the trees were over 12 inches in diameter. One tree landed on a car and destroyed it. Due to the significant damage to power lines, the power in Waconia was out for several hours.

A large bow echo surged across eastern Hennepin County causing numerous downed trees and power lines. Some of the trees were 12 inches in diameter. There were also several measured reports of severe wind gusts from private weather stations in Hennepin County. One measured wind gust was 58 knots. In addition, the Spirit of the Lakes Festival had shelters and tents blown down. The Spring Park City Hall had a tree blown down. At one point, 33,000 Xcel Energy customers were out of power in Hennepin County.
A large tree branch damaged a roof near Christmas Lake in Excelsior. Power was also out in Excelsior.
Several large trees were toppled northeast of Hugo.
A large tree was blown down in New Prague.
Several large trees were blown down with no power for several hours in Lino Lakes.

A severe squall line produced significant tree and power line damage across Dakota County from near the Scott, Dakota County border, through Lakeville, Burnsville, Apple Valley, Rosemount, and to Coates. Numerous large trees and tree limbs were blown down with some power outages. A few private weather stations measured wind speeds of 45 to 55 mph. One private weather station had a measured wind gust of 61 knots in Lakeville.

A severe squall line produced significant tree damage across Scott County from near Marystown, east-southeast toward Prior Lake and Credit River. Numerous trees were uprooted or toppled in sporadic areas. There were also several private weather stations that measured wind gusts of 45 to 55 mph from Shakopee to Prior Lake. There was also a measured wind gust of 58  mph in Belle Plaine, and 56 mph wind gust west of New Prague.

A storm survey indicated that an EF-0 tornado touch downed in the northwest portion of North Oaks, near Charley Lake, and moved east-northeast to the southern side of Deep Lake, where the greatest number of trees were toppled and snapped. Some of the trees fell on houses, vehicles and other structures. The tornado had a path length of 1.9 miles with maximum winds of 80 mph.

A storm survey indicated that an EF-1 tornado touched down in Hollywood Township in Carver County. The tornado spun up seven miles west-southwest of Watertown and continued east-northeast to two miles west-southwest of Watertown. The most damage occurred as the tornado crossed Vega Avenue where numerous trees were snapped and some minor structural damage was found. An apple orchard was also damaged with this tornado. There was a private weather station that measured a 99 mph wind gust before it blew off the roof. The path length was 5.1 miles long with a maximum wind speed of 105 mph.

A storm survey indicated a significant downburst caused damage west of Goodhue. Severe downburst winds initially caused damage to a barn and outbuildings at a farm about 9 miles west of Goodhue. Farther east, about 7.5 miles west of Goodhue, there were numerous trees blown down, an empty grain bin was destroyed, tin was blown off some outbuildings, doors were blown off a machine shed, and some corn was destroyed. These were the two hardest hit locations. Between the two locations, there were just a few trees or large branches taken down. Both locations exhibited divergent damage patterns indicative of a downburst. Based on the survey damage, the highest winds were around 80 to 85 mph.

A landspout-type tornado briefly occurred north of Ormsby. A storage building and some piles of tiling were damaged as the tornado hit a construction business. The tornado was photographed or recorded on video by several people.
Several large tree limbs were blown down in the neighborhood of Minnehaha Avenue and White Bear Avenue in northeast St. Paul.
A few trees were blown down in the city of Hancock.
A snowmobile trailer was blown into a roadway behind a local business in Morris.

A storm survey indicated an EF-1 occurred near Eau Galle, Wisconsin. The EF-1 tornado formed one mile northwest of Eau Galle, and continued generally east to four miles east of Eau Galle. Most of the damage was down trees and power lines. The greatest damage occurred just north of Eau Galle, where trees were snapped and uprooted, and a home weather station reported a maximum wind gust of 88 mph. The maximum width was 50 yards and was on the ground for approximately 5.3 miles.
Several trees were snapped and uprooted east of Chippewa Falls on County Road K.
A Cul-De-Sac was flooded off Townsvalley Road.
Water was running out of a drainage ditch and over Coulee Trail, one half mile east of Highway 35. The water eventually washed the road out.
Flood waters damaged a shoulder of County Road U near Glover Road.
Flood waters closed Highway 12 near Knapp for several hours.
Flood waters closed part of the road near the intersection of Highway 170 and County Road N.
A CoCoRaHS observer measured 6.50 inches in a 4 hour period just south of River Falls.
A CoCoRaHS observer measured 7.31 inches of rain in a 5 hour period north of River Falls.
A measured rainfall report of 7.10 inches occurred east of Hudson.
A measured rainfall report of 6.54 inches occurred in River Falls.
A measured rainfall report of 5.67 inches occurred east of Eagleton.
The Troy Glen Trailer Park (consisting of about 20 homes) was evacuated to the Troy Town Hall due to flood waters, and the American Red Cross assisted in the displaced residents.
Flood waters closed the intersection of Highway K and 170th Street south of Cornell.

The Red Wing Fire Department reported a bolt of lightning caused a small fire of the exterior of a home at 1141 East Ave in Red Wing. The small fire was extinguished within minutes and no injuries were reported.

Fire damaged a home in Brooklyn Park early Monday morning. The fire was reported about 1 a.m. (12 am LST). No injuries were reported. The fire destroyed the attic and damaged parts of the second floor. The roof was also destroyed.

A fire was caused by lightning in Rosemount the morning of July 24th. The fire burnt the exterior of a fourplex south side. The fire eventually worked its way inside the building, but firefighters were able to get the flames under control quickly.

A St. Cloud home suffered minor fire damage caused by a lightning strike Tuesday morning, July 28th. Firefighters arrived to find a small fire that the homeowner had put out with an extinguisher. The fire department estimated damage to the house at $400, and reported no injuries.

Strong rear flank downdraft winds accompanied a tornado.  The winds tipped over two silos that landed on top of a barn about 4 miles south of Canby. The winds also toppled dozens of trees. Even after the tornado dissipated, strong winds continued eastward into the city of Porter, with occasional tree and crop damage along the way.
Several trees and a grain bin were blown over.
Lac Qui Parle state park officials reported trees and large branches toppled, including some falling on a building. The building was barely damaged.
Baseball size hail fell in Camp Ripley during the evening of Wednesday, August 12th. The next morning, golf ball size hail was still in the ditches where the large hail fell the night before.
A few large trees were blown down with one tree taking down a power line.
A few trees were uprooted north of Browerville on Highway 71.
Several power poles were toppled in the city of Vesta.
Several funnel clouds were reported north of New London.

Local officials in Isanti County indicated that non-thunderstorm wind gusts occurred around the city of Cambridge and caused several large tree limbs, and small trees to blow down and block city roads. No injuries were reported.

The St. James airport AWOS measured a wind gust of 59 knots. In addition, a Minnesota Department of Transportation traffic and weather sensor just west of the Watonwan, Cottonwood county line, had a measured wind gust of 73 mph at 7:03 am LST. This sensor also reported sustained winds of 40 to 50 mph for over a half hour.

The Minnesota Department of Transportation has a traffic and weather instrument on Highway 60 just east of Madelia, Minnesota. This wind sensor measured a wind gust of 60 mph, with sustained winds of 40 to 50 mph from 6:50 to 7:30 am LST. In addition, local officials reported a wide area of tree branch debris across Blue Earth County.
Outflow from a decaying thunderstorm caused a large grain silo to be ripped off its foundation and crushed near Ceylon. In addition, a large tree blew down near Sherburn and destroyed a small shed.

A weak tornado touched down briefly, damaging several trees, a small lightweight greenhouse that was covered in plastic, and  removed a few shingles from two outbuildings. The tornado moved into a field and dissipated. Winds were estimated at about 65 mph.

A tornado knocked down about a dozen trees before entering a farm, where there was minor damage to eaves and soffits of the main building as well as to some outdoor furnishings. Winds were estimated at about 65 mph. The tornado was caught on video by a local storm chaser.
Rear flank downdraft winds accompanied a brief tornado. The wind damage was just west of the tornado and took down several trees and large branches, and also produced minor damage to outbuildings.
A large tree was blown down in southwest Willmar.
A garage was blown down and several trees were toppled.
A hardwood tree was snapped.
Several hardwood trees were snapped, six wooden power poles were snapped, and an irrigation system was tipped over.

A damage survey revealed that a rear flank downdraft (RFD) accompanied a tornado, and produced tree damage to the south of the tornado track.  Numerous trees were tipped over and large branches were broken.  Once the tornado dissipated about two miles west of Staples, the RFD broadened out and swept across the south side of Staples, where it continued to topple dozens of trees. The last damage noted from the RFD was southeast of Staples. Several outbuildings were damaged, and trees fell across many vehicles.
The tornado briefly touched down in a corn field and was caught on video by multiple storm chasers.  It was also witnessed by fire department personnel.
The tornado briefly touched down in a corn field and was caught on video by multiple storm chasers.

There was a brief touchdown just north of Norway Lake. It was mostly over an open field, but it did hit a couple trees. The tornado was filmed by multiple storm chasers and witnessed by fire department personnel.

A tornado touched down and grazed the southern edge of the community of Hawick.  It ripped up and tossed a few trees and partially removed metal from the roofs of storage sheds or other outbuildings.  It was filmed by multiple storm chasers.
There was a brief touchdown just north of Games Lake. It was over an open field, and was filmed by multiple storm chasers.
The hail was photographed.

Local county officials, trained observers and the general public indicated widespread flooding across portions of northern Dunn County. Numerous roads were either closed or partially closed during the height of the flood event. The village of Ridgeland was inundated with flood waters, and some roads were impassable. Rainfall reports in the area had averaged between 4 to 6 inches, with locally 8 inches near Ridgeland. ||Specifically, flooding was reported on Highway 25, County Roads W and WW near Ridgeland. Other parts of Dunn County, including Highway Q at 129th St, and Highway S, east of Highway HH, were closed. ||Several of the roads were damaged around Ridgeland and south to southeast toward the Dunn/Chippewa County line.

Local county officials, trained observers, and the general public indicated widespread flooding across portions of northwest and western Chippewa County as locally 4 to 6 inches of rain fell in less than 3 hours. Several roads were closed during the height of the storm, plus the city of Chippewa Falls had some problems with flooded roadways. In addition, five feet of water was reported in the basement of one residence in Chippewa Falls and at St. Joseph's Hospital in Chippewa Falls. In addition, County Highway S was closed east of the U.S. Highway 53 due to a washout. Other roads in Chippewa county, including Highway C and State Highway 40, and Highway T at the Highway N intersection, were closed due to flood waters.
Flood waters covered the intersection of Route D and Route HH near Clear Creek.

Local officials reported several roads closed across southern Eau Claire County due to excessive rainfall, with amounts of 3 to 5 inches in a 3 hour period. Several culverts were damaged along Highway 53 and Highway 12 near Augusta. State officials estimated that there was about $300,000 in road damage in Eau Claire County.
Several streets were flooded in the town of Wells.

Parts of 9th Avenue between 5th and County Road P, near Arland, were washed out due to excessive rainfall. Significant street flooding was noted at 15th Avenue and west of 10th Avenue near Poskin, along the Vermillion River. In addition, there were reports of water over the road north of Barron, near the Yellow River.

Several reports of stalled cars along I-35 from Eagan, northeast to West St. Paul. This was noted on Minnesota Department of Transportation Webcams that noted the stalled cars and deep water in the roadway.

Several webcams from the Minnesota Department of Transportation indicated stalled cars in deep water along I-35E in St. Paul north of the Mississippi River. There were also reports of street flooding around the city of St. Paul, and northeast to North St. Paul.

Several reports on media and on social media had significant flooding along the Como Creek, near Bloomer. It closed parts of Highway 40, along the creek, west of Bloomer for several hours in the morning. In addition, a social media picture had street flooding on Duncan Creek in the town of Bloomer. The flood waters also had covered up Bloomer High School practice football field, a baseball field and the old playground for elementary school.
Excessive rainfall amounts of 3 to 6 inches occurred in parts of Polk County which led to roads washed out and closed. Two of the roads were near Clayton.

A tornado moved out of Wadena County (where it was rated EF2) and into Todd County.  A barn was collapsed just south of Aldrich, with roofing material blown 1/2 mile downwind. Dozens of trees were broken or uprooted in this area. Several wooden power poles were snapped. An outbuilding was also destroyed. Farther east, an outbuilding was destroyed along with a roof partially blown off near the intersection of 500th street and 223rd Avenue, just northwest of Dower Lake.  Significant tree damage was noted on the northeast side of Dower Lake, and concentrated damage continued in a path to about two miles west of Staples. Separate entries have also been made for numerous trees blown down due to the rear flank downdraft and downbursts north of the tornado track.
A lightning strike destroyed the cross atop St. Helena���s Catholic Church which crashed to the ground and caused more damage to the marble steps.
A lightning strike damaged a bell tower at the St. Cloud Children's Home that was built in 1924.

Trained weather observers and local officials indicated that 6 to 10 inches fell across Lac Qui Parle County, with the heaviest in Madison at 9.6 inches. The storm started on November 30th with a period of 3 to 5 inches that fell during the afternoon of Monday, November 30th.
Trained weather observers and local officials indicated that 6 to 8 inches fell across Brown County, with the heaviest near Springfield.
Trained weather observers and local officials indicated that 7 to 9 inches fell across Redwood County. Locally, the town of Redwood Falls measured 8.6 inches of snow.
Trained weather observers and local officials indicated that 7 to 8 inches fell along the Redwood, Renville county line near Morton.
Trained weather observers and local officials indicated that 7 to 9 inches fell across Yellow Medicine County.

Trained weather observers and local officials indicated that 6 to 10 inches fell across Lac Qui Parle County, with the heaviest in Madison at 9.6 inches. This storm had snowfall before midnight, and continued into the early morning of December 1st.

Trained weather observers and local officials indicated that 6 inches of snow fell in a 12 hour period from the afternoon of November 30th, to the early morning of December 1st. Both Montevideo and Watson measured 6 inches of snow.

Trained weather observers and local officials indicated that 6 inches of snow fell in a 12 hour period from the afternoon of November 30th, to the early morning of December 1st. An individual measured 6 inches of snow north of Willmar.

Trained weather observers and local officials indicated that 6 inches of snow fell in a 12 hour period from the afternoon of November 30th, to the early morning of December 1st. Both Montevideo and Watson measured 6 inches of snow.

Trained weather observers and local officials indicated that 6 inches of snow fell in a 12 hour period from the afternoon of November 30th, to the early morning of December 1st. A local observer measured 6 inches of snow north of Willmar.

A tornado moved across several farmsteads, destroying several outbuildings, uprooting or breaking hundreds of trees, and damaging crops. No one was injured.

The tornado near Litchfield was rated an EF-2 with peak winds of 115 mph. It had a maximum width of 100 yards and traveled approximately 3.2 miles. The tornado caused a lot of tree damage, though three single family homes received significant roof damage, and a double wide manufactured home, and garage were flipped and rolled. Another garage and shed were destroyed near Highway 12 on the north side of town.

The tornado near Watkins was also rated an EF-2 with peak winds of 125 mph. It had a maximum width of 400 yards and traveled approximately 2.1 miles. One injury occurred with this tornado. The first significant damage was to a business along Highway 55 on the south side of town. The tornado then tracked across the highway and passed through the St. Anthony Cemetery before passing through the center of Watkins doing damage to structures and many trees. The most significant damage occurred between Stearns Ave and Meeker Ave where several homes had significant roof damage, and had detached sheds, and garages destroyed. The tornado exited the town and did further tree damage as the tornado moved northeast into Stearns County.

The tornado north of Watkins in Stearns County was rated an EF-1 with peak winds of 105 mph. It had a maximum width of 250 yards and traveled approximately 4.0 miles. This tornado was spawned by the same storm that moved through Watkins. Multiple chaser videos showed the Watkins tornado lifted off the ground as the parent storm became occluded, and a new tornado developed shortly thereafter, with its touchdown point made visible by the presence of corn laid down in a field south of the first homestead hit. This was about two-thirds of a mile north-northeast of where the Watkins tornado lifted. At the first farmstead to be hit, two open air cattle sheds were completely destroyed, along with a metal storage shed and two mostly empty grain bins. There were two cattle killed at this location as well. This storm destroyed more outbuildings at a farmstead along 160th street, with the rest of the damage along the path of the tornado being corn laid flat and tree damage.

This is the continuation track of the Watkins tornado in Meeker County as it moved northeast and dissipated near County Road 143rd. As the tornado moved into Stearns County a farmstead outside of town was hit before lifting shortly thereafter. While in Stearns County, this tornado was rated an EF0 with maximum winds of 65 mph and a width of 100 yards, but when it was in Meeker County, it was rated EF2.

A mesocyclone that was sometimes three miles wide caused widespread wind damage, knocking down trees, destroying sheds and causing other building damage.  The downburst wind damage from the mesocyclone was mostly spread across a 1.5 mile wide area, but occasionally reached a width of three miles.  There was also a tornado embedded within the mesocyclone (see separate entry for the tornado).

A mesocyclone originated in Pierce County and caused widespread downburst damage across a 1.5 mile wide area.  It knocked down many hundreds of trees, and partially removed the roof off of one house.  The mesocyclone continued into Pepin County, where it continued to produce wind damage and then a tornado (see separate entries for Pepin County).
