A measured wind gust of 85 mph occurred near Union Hill. A barn roof was also blown off near the measured wind gust. In addition, a NWS storm survey concluded that straight-line winds produced the damage in the area.
Several large trees were blown down in New Prague, plus a road sign was blown down at the intersection of Highway 13, and 19, east of New Prague.
A large tree was blown down, and landed on a home in Heidelberg.
Several power lines were blown down on Iago Blvd southeast of Belle Plaine.
A large tree was blown down north of New Prague.
A large tree was blown down north of Union Hill.
A few trees were blown down at 200th Street and Harlow.
There was sporadic tree damage, up to 8 inches in diameter, on the east side of Cedar Lake.
A few trees were blown down between Burnsville and Rosemount, in Dakota County.
Several trees were damaged on the west side of Red Wing.
An eight inch diameter tree was blown down in Faribault.
A few power lines were blown down on the 26400 Block of German Road, southwest of Belle Plaine.
Power lines were blown down in the city of Arlington.
A tree blew down on a trailer in Le Center.
A swath of large hail, up to quarter size, fell around Hanley Falls.
Several trees and power lines were blown down between Lakeville, and Farmington.
A swath of large hail, up to ping pong ball size, fell along the Scott, Rice County border, northeast to near County Road 2, and 27, west of Elko New Market.
A swath of large hail, up to golf ball size fell north of Lonsdale, near Veseli. The hail damaged several tin roofs, a pole barn, and vehicles in the area.
There were several reports of large hail, up to quarter size, around Red Wing and the Hay Creek area. Some damage occurred to roofs.

Several pictures from social media showed large trees blown down from the University of Wisconsin, Eau Claire campus, south and east across the southern part of the city. A few trees landed on homes and caused damage to their roofs.
A large tree limb broke off, and damaged a camper and truck.
A large tree blew down on a power line south of Motley.

St. James regional airport measured a wind gust of 78 mph.  A storm survey team from the NWS determined the damage from surrounding areas was due to a downburst, with a classic fanning out pattern. Part of a roof from a turkey barn was blown off, several vehicles were blown off Highway 60, and hundreds of trees were broken or uprooted southwest to southeast of the airport. There was also significant damage to the airport's hanger.
A social media picture posted a large tree that was blown down in Delano.
A firefighter observed a funnel cloud moving near their home.

There were a few reports of downed trees and power lines near Crystal Airport, and Edina. Measured wind gusts from the decaying thunderstorm complex in west central Wisconsin were between 40 and 50 mph around the Twin Cities metro area. There was a measured wind gust at the MSP airport of 52 mph during the morning event.
Several trees were blown down near Vineland.
A large tree was blown down near 525th and Fairfield Avenue in Rush City.
A trained spotter measured a wind gust from his private weather station of 60 mph.
Numerous trees were blown down on houses and vehicles, along with power lines in Glencoe.
In the city of Arlington, a large tree blew down on power lines on Meadowbrook Lane.
A large two foot diameter tree was blown down in Lester Prairie.
A large tree blew down on a vehicle in the city of Norwood/Young America.
Several trees were blown down over County Road 50 near East Union.
A storm chaser observed a brief touchdown in an open field east of Hollandale.
In the city of Wells, several large branches, and a tree were blown down in the city park.
In the city of Jordan, a tree and several large tree branches blew down in Lagoon Park.
Local officials reported several trees blown down in the city of Willmar.

A NWS Storm Survey indicated that an EF0 tornado touched down on the west side of Fireside Lake, on Mud Lake Road. This tornado tracked approximately 7.6 miles northeast, before lifting on the east side of the Flambeau River, west of Sheep Camp Road. The tornado was on the ground for 14 minutes with a path width of 100 yards, and a maximum wind speed of 85 mph. Numerous trees were blown down or uprooted along the path. A few trees blew down on lake cabins causing considerable damage. No injuries occurred with this event.
Multiple storm chasers observed and filmed a brief tornado in an open field.

A NWS Storm Survey indicated no area of concentrated damage in Arlington, Minnesota. There was damage to several dozen trees around town. In addition, a small portion of a roof was blown off in Arlington. Damage was not concentrated in any area, and was deemed most likely to have occurred from downburst winds.
A storm chaser filmed a brief tornado that touched down in an open field.
A measured wind gust from a local trained spotter.
A local measured wind gust of 58 mph from the Emergency Manager.
Several trees and power lines were blown down in Belview.
A 20 foot tall tree was snapped, and fell onto a minivan in Gaylord.
A large tree was blown over, and fell onto an apartment building causing some structural damage in Norwood/Young America.
A large tree blew down in Arlington.
A large tree was snapped off on 80th Street, and Babcock Avenue, southeast of Glencoe.
Numerous large tree branches, and trees up to one foot in diameter, were blown down around Belle Plaine.
A trained spotter measured 2.25 inches of rain in less than an hour.
A spotter measured a wind gust of 73 mph. A few trees were uprooted near the location of the measured wind gust.
A few large tree branches were blown down near Carlos.
A large tree was blown down by Como Park, near Hamline Avenue, and Nebraska.
A large tree was blown down in Shakopee.
A large tree fell between two houses in North St. Paul.
A tree was uprooted on Harriet Island.
A 14 inch diameter tree branch was blown down, blocking Lexington Parkway.
Several trees were blown down near Highway 13 in Savage.
Several trees were blown down near County Road 21 & 18.
Several trees were blown down near Highway 169, and County Road 21.
A large tree was blown down in Dellwood, off of White Bear Lake.
A light pole was blown down near Highway 101.
Several large tree branches were blown down north of White Bear Lake.
There were multiple reports of large hail, some up to 2 inches in diameter, on the northeast side of Delano, at Lake Rebecca.
A few trees were blown down on the east side of Lake Wissota, in Chippewa Falls.
Several power lines were blown down, and a 12 inch diameter pine tree was snapped.
Flash flooding occurred on the westbound lane of I-394, near Penn Avenue. Flood waters were up to 2 feet deep.
Flash flooding with up to two feet of water on Lake Street near Lake Calhoun.
Flash flooding, with water up to two feet deep, occurred near I-94, and I-35W.
Numerous roads were flooded in the Uptown area of Minneapolis. Social media pictures indicated flood waters, nearly 3 feet high around the area.
Large hail, up to baseball size, fell across the southern part of Prior Lake, northeast through Credit River Township, and up to Savage in Scott County.
This is the continued path of very large hail that moved from Scott County, into Dakota County. Up to ping pong size hail continued to fall into Dakota County near the I-35W, and I-35E interchange.

A swath of large hail, up to golf ball size, occurred from northwest of Chokio, to Donnelly. There were reports of larger hail, but no pictures were available. Damage occurred to vehicles, buildings (siding, rain gutters & shingles), and crops.
The swath of large hail continued through the rest of Stevens County to the Douglas County line. The largest hail stone measured was golf ball size.

Numerous reports of large hail occurred from north of Farwell, to north of Forada, and south of Osakis. The largest hail stone was golf ball size north of Forada. This is the continuation of the long hail swath that developed across Stevens County, and moved into far northwest Pope County, before entering Douglas County near Farwell.

This is the continuation of a swath of large hail that developed across Stevens County, and moved northeast across northwest Pope, southeast Douglas, and over the southern part of Todd County. There was a measured report of golf ball size hail north of West Union. This swath of large hail continued to north of Swanville.

There were numerous reports of large hail, up to baseball size, that occurred across parts of Morrison County. Hail was reported near Cushing, then east-southeast to Randall, Camp Ripley area, and north of Freedhem. The same line of storms moved southeast to near Hillman, but no additional reports of hail was observed. However, the emergency managers did have reports of trees and power lines down across central Morrison County.

There was a large swath of trees and power lines blown down from north of Ogilvie, on the Mille Lacs, and Kanabec County line, southeast to north of Grasston. There was also damage that occurred around Mora.

The bow echo that moved across Pine County, continued to intensify. It moved from the northern part of Chisago County, southeast into Polk County in Wisconsin. The path of straight line winds was noted as it crossed interstate 35 where very large trees were uprooted or blown down. There was damage to barns, outbuildings and homes along the path. The Chisago County fair grounds was closed due to blown down trees and power lines in Rush City.

The intense bow echo entered Polk County in the far northwest corner. It moved southeast and caused significant damage to trees and power lines along its path. A trained spotter measured a wind gust of 73 knots in Cushing. This individual also measured sustained winds of nearly 70 mph for 5 minutes.
There were multiple reports of downed trees, up to three feet in diameter, across parts of Northfield.
A large tree was blown down near the airport.
Wind gust measured by a home weather station. In addition, several large tree branches were blown down.
Power was knocked out in the city of St. James due to blown down power lines.
The Minnesota Department of Transportation weather sensor reported a measured wind gust of 52 knots.
A trained spotter measured a wind gust of 52 knots.

This slow moving tornado was widely photographed and caught on video by multiple citizens and storm spotters. It hit several farmsteads, breaking or uprooting dozens of trees. One open air building on a feedlot was destroyed. Several machine sheds had doors blown out, and tin was peeled off the portion of several roofs.
This tornado mostly moved across open fields, but it did strike one farmstead.  About one dozen trees were broken and minor structural damage occurred to several outbuildings.
This tornado touched down in an open field.
The Steele County Sheriff filmed a brief landspout tornado over an open field.
There was a picture of wind, and hail damage to a home in Glencoe.
There were numerous power lines that were damaged, 3 were snapped, and several large tree limbs, up to 10 inches in diameter, were blown down from near Olivia, to Hector.
The Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe Tribal Emergency Management showed a few trees that were blown down in the city of Onamia.
The four inch diameter hailstone was measured with a ruler, and posted on social media.
A picture from social media with the baseball sized hailstone.
There were numerous pictures from social media on the large hailstone.
The hailstones caused major damage to cars, a camper and siding near 92nd Avenue, and Hampshire Avenue in Brooklyn Park.
Several trees were blown down in Blaine.
A tree was snapped in half near Centerville.
A few trees were snapped in half around Burnsville.
A large tree was uprooted in Savage.
A large tree was uprooted near Hampton. The tree caused roof damage.
A large tree limb was snapped, and a 15 foot trailer was blown over in Cannon Falls.
A barn was damaged due to severe straight-line winds near Manchester.
There was a measured rainfall report of 3.44 inches near Belview.
There was a measured rainfall report of 5.15 inches near Redwood Falls.
There was a measured rainfall report of 4.14 inches south of Bird Island.
There was a measured rainfall report of 3.15 inches near Bechyn.

There was an unconfirmed report of 7 inches of rainfall around the Morton area. There were also measured rainfall amounts of 3 to 6 inches around the area. Due to the extreme rainfall amounts, and the impact of the area, approximately 30 homes were flooded from local small streams and runoff. Three homes had 6-8 feet of water in their basements, and Minnesota Highway 19 was closed east of Morton due to a mudslide.

A fire department spotter reported hail as large as two inches fell for around 15 minutes at Lake Hanska County Park.  Nearby, Prairie Grounds Campground was also hit, with one camper totaled and another camper had hail punch holes through its plastic roof vents. A pontoon was also significantly damaged. Some crops in the area were destroyed.
A large tree branch broke off and landed on a vehicle. There was considerable damage to the car.

The Minnesota National Guard relayed pictures and an account of a flash flood that went through Camp Ripley during the evening of July 14th.  It began approximately 7:15 PM CST. During the height of the event, water flowed through buildings and the latrine. The depth of the water was up to 2 feet deep, and cars were stranded in parking lots. There were also reports outside of the camp of washed out roadways.
Several trees were blown down near the intersection of Mahogany Street, and Riverdale Road, southeast of Mora.
There were reports of hail throughout the county, with the largest hailstone being ping pong ball size in Little Falls.
There were several reports of downed trees and power lines from Pierz, to Hillman.
A swath of large hail fell along the the Pope, Swift County line. The largest hail stone reported was golf ball size. Damage occurred to corn fields along the path.

The Farm Service Agency office for Redwood County indicated a one to three mile wide swath of hail as large as golf balls fell across southeastern Redwood County, with many crops heavily damaged or destroyed. Time estimated based on radar.
Dozens of trees knocked down, including some on houses, sheds and vehicles. A roof was partially off a machine shed. An aerial photo shows the latter portion of the path was through a corn field.

This tornado started in Polk County and dissipated in Barron County. A damage survey and aerial photos showed many hundreds of trees down from the tornado, which was surrounded by a massive area of severe downburst winds that downed thousands of trees. The tornado itself knocked down sheds, took roofs off barns and    outbuildings, and snapped or knocked down trees, some of which landed on houses and vehicles.

This tornado started in Polk County and ended in Barron County. It knocked down hundreds of trees in Barron County, some of which fell on houses, garages,  outbuildings and vehicles. The tornado was surrounded by a massive area of severe downburst winds that downed thousands of trees.
A tornado hit a large storage shed, taking off part of its roof and blowing in garage doors.  It also knocked over a few trees, and entered a corn field, where it dissipated.

A tornado touched down on the southwest side of Bone Lake and moved north-northeast, knocking down hundreds of trees, some of which landed on houses, sheds and vehicles. The tornado also hit several farms, taking the roof off a barn, machine shed, and outbuildings, and knocking over a silo.
A storm chaser was 5 miles southeast of Fairmont, and reported a brief touchdown 1 mile northwest of his location in an open field. No damage was reported, but it appeared visually to have been weak.

An EF0 tornado developed 3 miles southwest of Biscay and tracked northeast to just north of Biscay, Minnesota before dissipating. Corn was flattened along the path and some trees were uprooted near Minnesota Highway 22, and 150th Street. The maximum wind speed was estimated at 85 mph.
A brief EF0 tornado spun up southeast of Silver Lake and produced a little damage to some trees.

An EF1 tornado spun up southeast of Silver Lake and quickly became 1/4 mile wide (440 yards), as it tracked northeast across Highway 7 before dissipating 3 miles east-northeast of Silver Lake. Corn was flattened, a few outbuildings were destroyed, and many trees were damaged.

An EF1 tornado spun up on the southwest side of Sylvan Lake and continued northeast in a broken path through Bone Lake, and moved into Chisago County on 240th Street North, east of Morgan Avenue. The path length was approximately 4.4 miles across Washington County, with a maximum width of 440 yards. The worst damage occurred on Bone Lake where numerous large trees were uprooted or blown down. Some roof damage was noted, but most of the trees fell away from homes. Other damage along the path was associated with flattened corn, tree damage, a storage shed that had its roof blown off, and damage to a solar panel farm.

This is the continuation path of the Washington County tornado that moved into Chisago County on 240th Street North, east of Morgan Avenue. This EF1 tornado continued for approximately another 3.8 miles before dissipating north of a farm that was damaged on 268th Street. Along the path in Chisago County, the tornado damaged a farm shed, uprooted numerous trees, damaged an outdoor wedding venue near Highway 25, and destroyed an outbuilding before dissipating. Maximum winds were estimated at 90 mph, with a width of 250 yards in Chisago County.
A funnel cloud was observed south of Sunburg.
A funnel cloud was observed near Rosendale.
A funnel cloud was observed for four minutes, but did not touch the ground near Bernadotte.
A funnel cloud was observed near Eagle Lake.
A funnel cloud was observed near Madison Lake.
A funnel cloud was observed near Lemond.
There were two separate reports of a funnel cloud near White Rock.
In addition to the large hail stone, there was a power pole blown down in Waseca.
The hail lasted for 15 minutes, but the largest hail stone was ping pong size.
A trained spotter filmed a brief touchdown.  It moved across a tree line, uprooting a few trees and breaking large branches. No other damage was reported.

Multiple storms chasers, spotters and citizens filmed and photographed this tornado. It mostly moved across fields, and there was minor damage to one soybean field. It blew a portable hoop barn across a field. There was a two mile gap in the middle of its path where it did not appear to be in contact with the ground, but video and pictures show the parent funnel cloud remained consistently evident.

A NWS storm survey indicated that an EF-0 tornado touched down along 300th Street, where trees were damaged near a farm and a barn was pushed over. The worst damage occurred at at home along 290th Street where a detached garage was pushed off its foundation. Maximum winds were estimated at 80 mph.

A NWS storm survey indicated that an EF-1 tornado touched down in a field just east of Mille Lacs County Road 4, and tracked to the southeast. EF-1 damage occurred along 70th Avenue where a large pole barn was completely destroyed. A nearby home also saw about half of its roof decking lifted off. Dozens of trees were broken or uprooted. The maximum winds were estimated at 90 mph.
A large tree blew down near Butterfield and caused a gas leak. No injuries were reported.
Several power lines were blown down in the city of St. James.
Several power lines were blown down in Madelia, and between St. James and Madelia.
A few large tree limbs were blown down in Winnebago.
A large tree blew down in Mapleton and damaged a transformer.
A few trees were blown down in Mankato.
A large tree fell on a house in Janesville.
A tree was blown down in the city of Albert Lea.
There was a social media image of half dollar size hail that fell near Morgan.
Local law enforcement officials barricaded numerous roads in the Owatonna area due to high water.
Local law enforcement officials barricaded parts of 410th and 120th street due to water over the road.
Local law enforcement officials barricaded 415th and 90th Street due to water over the road.
Local law enforcement officials barricaded 415th and 105th Street due to water over the road.
Local law enforcement officials barricaded County Road 6 and 305th Street due to water over the road.
A trained spotter measured 4 inches of rainfall in an hour.
Areas near, and surrounding the Crystal Shopping Center, and the 5700 Block of Broadway, were closed to to high water. Also, the 5600 Block of Corvallis Avenue was closed due to high water.
Local officials closed 42nd Avenue in New Hope due to flooding.
Local officials closed Preserve Blvd, and Anderson Lakes Parkway due to flooding.
Local officials closed parts of Hemlock Lane in Maple Grove due to flooding.
A few trees were snapped in Lakeville.
A local mesonet site measured 3.55 inches of rainfall in Medina.
A local observer measured 3.78 inches of rainfall near Hamel.
A local observer measured 4.00 inches of rainfall east of Plymouth.
A local observer measured 5.16 inches of rainfall north of Hamel.
A local observer measured 3.45 inches of rainfall south of Plymouth.
A local observer measured 3.85 inches of rainfall north of Plymouth.
A local observer measured 3.20 inches of rainfall near Lakeville.

Several trees were blown down between Anoka, Coon Rapids, Andover and Blaine. In addition to the trees, several power lines and street signs were damaged. There were also reports of minor tree damage around Lino Lakes, Fridley, Oak Grove and Lexington.
A NWS Storm Survey indicated straight-line wind damage to a farmstead and a few large trees uprooted.

A NWS Storm Survey indicated a tornado touchdown southeast of Belle Plaine, and tracked a quarter of a mile to the northeast. It damaged a farm and uprooted several large trees. Maximum winds were estimated at 80 mph.

A NWS Storm Survey indicated wind damage occurred north of Bruce, and tracked eastward for several miles. The wind downed numerous trees, damaged a barn and outbuilding northwest of Ladysmith. Winds were estimated up to 75 mph as most of the barn roof was damaged or lifted off.
A Minnesota Department of Transportation wind sensor measured a wind gust of 65 mph.
A measured wind report by a private weather station.
A measured wind report from a private weather station.
A measured wind report from a private weather station.
There were numerous reports of downed trees in the Little Falls area.
A roof was blown off a building south of Pierz.
There were reports of scattered trees blown down around Princeton.
Several reports of large tree branches and tree damage in Andover.

The local emergency manager indicated that the worst damage in the entire county was around Coon Rapids and Blaine. There were numerous trees blown down in the area, and reports of a few metal poles, and power lines that were blown down.
Several reports of multiple trees blown down, or uprooted in the Lino Lakes area.
Several reports of multiple trees blown down in the White Bear Lake area.

A brief tornado occurred just southwest of Howard Lake, MN. The tornado damaged 3 properties, with 2 barns heavily damaged and a private residence with shingles ripped off along with numerous trees snapped along the path of the tornado.

A NWS Storm Survey determined an EF0 tornado developed east of Watertown near County Road 20, and moved southeast into Hennepin County, north of Timber Creek Golf Course. Most of the damage was consistent with EF0 damage with numerous trees blown down or uprooted along its path.  The path length in Carver County was 1.3 miles, with a maximum width of 90 yards. The tornado was also confirmed by the MPX radar in real time given the Tornado Debris Signature sampled by the radar.

This is the continuation of the Carver County tornado that moved into Hennepin County northeast of Timber Creek Golf Course.  The storm survey determined an EF1 tornado occurred in Hennepin County where trees, crops, and a few machine sheds or outbuildings were damaged or blown down. ||The path length in Hennepin County was 2.5 miles, making the tornado total path length of 3.87 miles. The maximum width in Hennepin County was 210 yards, with a maximum wind speed of 90 mph. ||This tornado was also confirmed by the MPX radar in real time given the Tornado Debris Signature sampled by the radar.

A storm spotter photographed a funnel that seemed to be close to the ground. It may have touched down but the chaser was too far away (12 miles across rolling terrain) and noted no debris cloud. Nobody who was closer to the storm saw the funnel touch down.
A swath of large hail, with a measured report of quarter size near Farwell, occurred across northwest Pope County.
The local emergency manager indicated that a few trees and power lines were blown down from southwest of Onamia, to the Kanabec County line.
The Wild River State Park had damage throughout their park area. Numerous trees were blown down and blocked roads in and out of the park.
There were pictures of damage in the city of Fairmont. This included a large tree that fell down on a truck, and a few trees uprooted.
A trained spotter reported a large tree limb blown down in the city of Winnebago.
There were multiple reports of downed trees in the city of Janesville.
Several large tree limbs were blown down around the city of Waldorf.
There were reports of multiple trees blown down around Waseca.
There were numerous blown down large tree limbs on the southwest corner of County Road 45, and 250th street south of Faribault.
Several trees and large tree branches were blown down east of Clarks Grove.
A large tree was snapped at its base in Ellendale.
There was widespread tree damage, and some roof damage to commercial buildings around Albert Lea, and then eastward toward Hayward, and Glenville.
There was a large tree that was uprooted in the city of Zumbrota.
A tree was uprooted at the Owatonna country club.

The bow echo continued southeast across Polk County where thousands of large trees were broken, uprooted or blown down. Many trees landed on houses, sheds, outbuildings, and vehicles. Many outbuildings were destroyed by wind, along with roofs off barns and sheds. The swath of wind damage was nearly ten miles wide, and some areas had entire sections of forest leveled.

Thousands of large trees were broken, uprooted or blown down. Some were two feet in diameter. Many trees landed on houses, sheds, outbuildings, and vehicles. Many outbuildings were destroyed by wind, along with roofs off barns and sheds. The swath of wind damage was nearly ten miles wide, and some areas had entire sections of forest leveled.

This is the continuation of the blow down, straight-line wind event that moved across parts Chippewa County from New Auburn, to east of Bloomer. Numerous large trees were uprooted or blown down along this path.

There were thousands of trees broken, blown down or uprooted in a swath that was about eight miles wide, with the north/south extent from northwest of Comstock to  Turtle Lake. The swath extended to the east-southeast to the southwest side of the city of Barron.  Many trees landed on sheds, vehicles and outbuildings. Many outbuildings were destroyed by wind, along with roofs off barns and sheds.

This is the continuation of the damage path of 70-80 mph straight-line winds or microbursts. The path was about ten miles wide. Several thousand trees were blown down, some on power lines, houses, vehicles, sheds and outbuildings, causing considerable damage in the eastern part of Barron County.

This is the continuation of the blow down, straight-line wind event that moved across parts of northern Dunn County, between Ridgeland, and Sand Creek. There were numerous reports of blown down trees and power lines.
A large tree blew down and landed on a van.
A large tree was uprooted and landed on a camper. An individual inside the camper was injured.

A NWS Storm Survey indicated that straight-line winds, up to 80 mph, occurred in a small part of far northeast Rusk County. Based on the survey, the damage path that occurred in Sawyer County, continued along the path into far northeast Rusk County. There were reports of numerous large trees blown down across this area.

The local emergency manager, and several other county officials indicated that the path of blown down trees continued across portions of northern, and central Chippewa County between Bloomer, and Otter Lake in the east.

A NWS Storm Survey determined a tornado began on the south side of Elk Mound, near the intersection of I-94, and South Holly Road. The tornado moved northeast, crossing I-94, and continued into Chippewa County as it crossed 10th Street, south of 560th Avenue. Most of the damage was EF0 in Dunn County where a barn lost its roof, and trees were uprooted or blown down. The path length in Dunn County was 2.3 miles long, with a maximum width of 250 yards.

This is the continuation track of the tornado in Dunn County that crossed 10th Street, south of 560th Avenue. As the tornado tracked northeast, the tornado intensified to an EF3 where considerable damage occurred near County Road X, or Highway 29, and 30th Street, or County Road M. The tornado crossed Highway 29, and move northeast until dissipating east of 50th Street, north of County Road X. ||Based on the NWS Storm Survey, the most significant damage occurred in Wheaton Township, or east of Elk Mound around the intersection of County Road M, and Highway 29. This area saw entire groves of trees leveled, some stripping of bark, and the destruction of several structures. The destruction of a metal building and two nearby homes were consistent with expected damage from winds of EF3 in strength.||The path length in Chippewa County was 4.7 miles, with a maximum width of 725 yards, or nearly a half mile wide. The maximum wind speed was near 150 mph.||There were three injuries with this tornado, but no fatalities.

Two storm chasers documented a tornado that mostly crossed open fields. A NWS storm survey revealed damage to some bean fields as well as about two dozen trees uprooted or broken. No structural damage was noted.
A storm chaser documented a funnel cloud. It was not possible from the video to determine whether it touched down, and there were no reports of damage, so it was deemed to have been a funnel cloud.
There was a swath of large hail, which moved from Le Sueur, northeast to around Heidelberg.

The city of Wanamingo was hit hard with severe wind gusts. There were numerous full size trees blown down, branches everywhere, and other assorted damage.  There was damage to one mobile home, plus damage to a few cars (broken windshields and dents) from falling trees.
Several trees and power lines were blown down around Zumbrota.
A local TV station reported damage to a building, and several large trees uprooted near Buffalo. These reports were relayed to the NWS through social media after the damage occurred.
A few large tree limbs were blown down north of St. Stephen.
A private weather station measured a wind gust of 55 knots.
A large tree blew down on a power line and caused a fire.
Several trees were uprooted north of Montgomery.
Several trees were blown down across 40th Avenue in Chippewa Falls. Some damage to homes also occurred.
A large tree blew down in Chippewa Falls.

There was sporadic wind damage that occurred across all of Meeker County, especially in towns and bigger cities based on emergency manager notes. Numerous trees were blown down or uprooted, including a tree that had a diameter of 2 feet. There was an overturned pontoon on Big Swan Lake and several power lines and/or power poles blown down.
Most of the hail that fell in Scott County between Belle Plaine, Jordan and New Prague was half inch hail or smaller. However, one report of quarter size hail occurred near Lydia.
A Minnesota Department of Transportation wind sensor measured a wind gust of 66 mph.
The local police department reported that an individual had disappeared in the Redwood River near the 100 block of West Bridge Street and was presumed dead from drowning.

Hundreds of trees were downed in a swath that was several miles wide across Rusk Township in the southwest corner of Rusk County. Some power lines were also downed, but no property damage was reported.

There were numerous reports of flooded or closed roadways due to water over the road across southern Nicollet County. There were multiple mud slides in the Minnesota River Valley, including one on Highway 169, south of St. Peter. There was also rushing water over 490th street at Highway 14, southeast of Nicollet.

Several roads were underwater across northwest Blue Earth County, including 206th, 105th, and 494th. A mudslide occurred at Highway 68 and County Road 42 at Judson, it was the result of the water flowing out of a drainage ditch/creek, 1/2 mile south on 42 that overflowed its banks where it turns and crosses County Road 42. It rushed through corn and hay fields carrying mud, parts of trees and deep fast moving water. On the west side it knocked flat a swath of shoulder high corn to pool along 68 and 42 because the culvert under hwy 68 couldn't handle the flow. There were other roads across northern and western parts of Blue Earth County, but the flooding was not as severe.

Torrential rainfall with measured amounts of over 9 inches occurred in the city of Little Falls, causing numerous roads, city and county, to close. The city of Little Falls had many roads and culverts washed out, with some structures receiving water.

Parts of St. Croix County received over 8 to 9 inches of rain causing flooding and washed out roads across the county. The worst areas that experienced significant flooding were the Kinnickinnic, Rush and Eau Galle Recreation River areas, and the towns of Hammond, Baldwin, Emerald, Glenwood City, and Cylon. ||Some of the specific roads that were closed or washed out during the height of the flooding were: 1000 Block of 190th Street in Baldwin, 2100 110th Avenue in Baldwin, Country Road TK, DD & 240th Street in Baldwin, Highway 12 & 220th Street in Baldwin Township, 2254 130th Avenue in Emerald, 2900 Block of 200th Avenue in Glenwood City, and West Blvd & Highway 65 in Roberts.||Unfortunately,  A man died after he lost control while driving on a water-covered road north of Baldwin near County Road E and Highway 63. At least five other motorists standing on the roofs of their cars were rescued from rushing water in that same location in the Baldwin area.||About $4 Million dollars in damages was due to 40 homes that sustained major damage and one that was destroyed when the foundation caved in. The other $4 Million dollars was due to bridge, highway and road damage.

There were numerous road closures, and culverts overwhelmed by flood waters across portions of Pierce County. Some specific closures included Highway 10 west of Ellsworth, County Road O along the Trimbelle River, and the towns of Martell and El Paso were severely flooded from the Rush River.  In addition, some crops were washed out around Spring Valley.

There were several roads that were closed across Dunn County due to the flooding. There was some mudslides noted between Lake Tainter and Wheeler. County Road W, north of Colfax, had one foot of flowing water over it during the height of the storm.

A storm survey that was conducted by the local emergency manager, and storm chasers, concluded that a downburst caused wind damage from 4 miles southwest of Donnelly, to 2 miles northeast of Donnelly. The damage field was 1/2 mile wide and all the damage was to the east/northeast. All the damage outside of Donnelly was scattered trees blown down and some crop damage. There were multiple buildings in the town of Donnelly that had damage. Some siding and many shingles were blown off downtown structures. Some trees fell onto houses and buildings. Two metal buildings had their tin roofs partially removed and one had a steel garage door blown in.

There were several reports of roads flooded due to rainfall amounts of 1 to 3 inches in a very short period of time. These heavy rainfall rates, combined with the urban area (mostly runoff from the streets), led to several flooded roads and a couple closures. Specifically, White Bear Avenue, Lakewood, and Maryland Streets were flooded at one point with stalled vehicles.

This is the continuation of the tornado that moved across southern Washington County, and into Wisconsin. The path of the tornado continued to move east-northeast before dissipating 1.7 miles southwest of River Falls, Wisconsin. Trees were uprooted along the continuous path which was 6.2 miles long.

A NWS Storm Survey indicated that an EF1 tornado occurred in far southern Washington County, in a rural area, north of Hastings, Minnesota.  ||The tornado spun up 5 miles north of Hastings, Minnesota, and tracked eastward for 3.2 miles until it moved across the St. Croix River, and into Wisconsin. Two inch hail was measured at the NWS office. Due to the large hail size and almost a continuous line of storms redeveloping in the same areas, many roofs and cars were damaged.

Numerous sources from social media pictures to trained spotters reported and measured very large hail for nearly 35 minutes from the Carver, Hennepin County line east to Eden Prairie, and Bloomington. The largest hailstone was measured at 1.25 inches in diameter and fell in West Bloomington. Radar suggested larger hail was possible, but there were no pictures or observations to indicate any larger hailstones. Many roofs and cars were damaged.
Severe hail slowly decreased in size as it moved across Bloomington, with the largest measured hail size of 1.25 inches.

One report of quarter size hail was observed near St. Michaels. However, based on radar and similar reports earlier in the evening, there were likely larger hailstones west of St. Michaels, near Pelican Lake, and eastward through the town.
There were a few reports of large hail, the largest measuring golf ball size, occurred west of Hanover, to the community of Hanover, and moved eastward over the Wright, Hennepin County line.

There were numerous reports of large hail, the largest measured at 2 inches in diameter, occurred across Wright County. Based on radar, and observations, there was a swath of hail between Buffalo, and Montrose, including the towns, that moved eastward toward the Hennepin County line near Rockford. There was also likely large hail west of Buffalo but due to the time of night and the rural area, there were no reports and is not included here.

There were numerous reports of very large hail, up to tennis ball size, that occurred from Rockford, east-southeast along Highway 55, toward Medina, and eastward to Plymouth. The largest hailstone was measured in the town of Loretto where the 2.5-inch diameter hail fell around 2325 LST. Damage was reported to roofs and cars.

Spotters reported one inch hail, but the size and severity of the hailstones decreased after 2345 LST as the storm moved toward a more populated area of the Twin Cities metro area. However, as the severity of the hail decreased, more downbursts and straight-line winds started to develop.

There were a few reports of large hail, up to golf ball size, the occurred around Edina and Richfield. Local radar indicated that the hail was likely more widespread in southern Hennepin County but due to the time of night it wasn't reported. There were also reports of tree limbs blown down across the area where the hail fell.

There were two reports of large hail in Scott County, the largest was in Spring Lake Township where a 1.75-inch diameter hailstone was measured. Radar indicated that the largest and most widespread area of hail fell south and east of Prior Lake, toward the Scott, Dakota County line.

This was the largest hailstone reported in Dakota County from this set of storms. Radar indicated that the hail was likely largest in size and areal extent from Eagan, eastward to Inver Grove Heights, and toward the Dakota, Washington County line.
There were several reports of large hail in the city of Buffalo, with the largest hailstone measured at 2 inches.
There was likely severe hail east into Hennepin County but the time of night and rural area kept reports minimal.

There was a measured hailstone of 1 inch in diameter south of Ogilvie. Local radar showed a wider area of higher returns west and east of Ogilvie where larger hail likely fell. There was measured hailstone of 1.5 inches in southern Pine County as the storm moved east of Kanabec County.
There was a picture of a 1.5-inch hailstone in Northfield.
There was likely larger hail to the west and north of Robbinsdale as local radar had higher returns in this area.

There was lots of wind damage in Red Wing where many trees and branches were blown down, including damage to roofs, and power outages throughout the city. There was a measured wind report from a private weather station of 61 mph west of Red Wing at 1635 LST.
A measured wind report from the Department of Transportation wind sensor.

Several large trees were blown down or uprooted from Canby, and eastward toward St. Leo, and likely farther to the east along Highway 68. Due to the very rural area, and farmland of Yellow Medicine County, damage was isolated.

There was damage in the city of Hanley Falls where a machine shed was blown down, with crop damage around the area. Upstream, and based on radar, isolated crop damage likely occurred from Hazel Run to Hanley Falls, and beyond as the core of the strongest winds moved across this area.

Numerous reports of downed trees and power lines from the eastern part of Granite Falls, eastward along Highway 212 to Sacred Heart. However, the damage became more sporadic eastward toward Sacred Heart.

Widespread wind damage occurred around the city of Granite Falls. Numerous trees, power lines and structural damage occurred in the city with the Yellow Medicine East School District main building sustaining major damage. The winds tore off the heating and ventilation systems on the roofs, opening the duct work to the rain. Water poured through the ventilation system and directly into classrooms, hallways and on equipment.  On the south side of the Minnesota River, the Granite Run golf course suffered significant damage to trees and their local restaurant.
A few large trees were blown down between Sacred Heart, and Renville, including a large tree that fell on a house in Renville.

There were multiple trees and power lines blown down from southwest of Cannon Falls, through Cannon Falls, and to the east of town.  There were 3-4 houses that had roof damage, one of the houses had their entire roof blown off on Pine Street. One privately owned wind sensor between Cannon Falls and Red Wing had a report of 88 mph, but damage was too isolated for that type of wind severity.
Several trees were blown down between Clarkfield to Hazel Run. Crop damage was also noted throughout the county.

Numerous trees and power lines were blown down on the north and northeast side of Granite Falls. There was a measured wind gust of 122 mph on a wind farm north of Granite Falls. However, this measurement was taken at 200 feet above the ground.
A measured wind report from a private weather sensor.

This tornado mostly moved over a soybean field, but did clip a grove of trees. Video of the tornado was filmed by a storm chaser.

An NWS survey found damage consistent with an EF-1 tornado in northeastern Todd County about 6 miles west of Cushing. The tornado touched down 0.2 miles northwest of Big Lake and traveled north-northeast for nearly 5.2 miles as it moved into Morrison County, near Lincoln. The most significant damage in Todd County was along Star Lake, where several hundred trees were broken and uprooted.

This is the continuation track of the tornado that moved across northeast Todd County, and into northwest Morrison County before dissipating. It did remove portions of metal roofs at two businesses in Lincoln.

A tornado damaged a garage that was rotated slightly, and its door was bowed out, and a few shingles were damaged. Other damage was associated with large tree limbs blown down along the tornado's path.

An NWS survey found EF-0 tornado damage along and south of Green Lake around Spicer. The county emergency manager reported portion of a metal roof was blown off near the beginning of the tornado.  As it moved northeast, dozens of trees were snapped, and docks along the lake sustained damage. The tornado was documented on several videos, and drone images also provided information on the damage path, including the ending point of the tornado.

An NWS survey found damage consistent with an EF-0 tornado in northern Morrison County about 7 miles northeast of Little Falls. The tornado traveled northeast for almost 6 miles snapping large tree branches, uprooting trees, and causing damage to a few outbuildings.

An NWS survey found damage consistent with an EF-0 tornado in McLeod County north of Brownton. Several trees were snapped, a trailer was overturned, and a metal grain silo wall was damaged and collapsed. There were numerous photos and videos of this tornado taken by storm chasers and shared on social media.

An NWS Survey found an EF-0 tornado began over a peninsula of the northern portions of Diamond Lake. The tornado tracked northeast to the Kandiyohi/Meeker County line, near 340th Street and 210th Street Southeast, and did move into Meeker County.||Video from two storm chasers and one law enforcement officer showed this tornado. A damage survey also used two drones to determine the exact damage path. The tornado moved mostly over corn and bean fields, but did hit numerous trees that were snapped or uprooted when it was in Kandiyohi County.

This is the continuation of the Kandiyohi tornado that moved into Meeker County near 340th Street and 210th Street Southeast. The tornado continued to the northeast damaging many trees and corn/bean fields before dissipating near Crow River. It moved across one farmstead but only produced minor damage to outbuildings. At one point, a law enforcement officer along the Meeker/Kandiyohi line reported and videod one tornado to his south and another to his east. This tornado was the one to his east.
An NWS survey indicated that an EF-0 tornado tracked over mostly fields and open land, but it did hit some trees, downing large tree branches. Downburst wind damage was noted adjacent to the tornado.

A NWS survey, plus storm chasers video indicated an EF-1 tornado across portions of eastern Kandiyohi County, or the Irving Township area. This tornado destroyed one large shed and heavily damaged another. Drone video indicated the exact track of the tornado as it moved into Meeker County.

This is the continuation track of the tornado that tracked across Kandiyohi County before dissipating shortly after moving into Meeker County.  At one point, a law enforcement officer along the Meeker/Kandiyohi line reported and videod one tornado to his south and another to his east. This tornado was the one to his south.

An NWS survey found damage consistent with an EF-1 tornado in Mcleod County between Biscay and Glencoe. Maximum wind speeds of 95 MPH snapped and uprooted several trees and damaged outbuildings. There were numerous photos and videos of this tornado shared on social media.

An NWS survey found damage consistent with an EF-0 tornado in eastern Morrison county about 2 miles southeast of Hillman. It traveled east-northeast for nearly 3 miles uprooting trees along its path. It moved across one farmstead with the only damage being to uprooted trees.

An EF-0 tornado mostly tracked across corn fields, but it did strike a grove of trees and knock down some large tree limbs before dissipating northeast of Lake Minnie Belle. There was also downburst winds around this tornado that occurred west of the path, and just north of the lake between 205th Street, and 624th Avenue.

An NWS Survey indicated a brief EF-0, which was also observed by people nearby. The tornado touched down just off shore on the western edge of Reitz Lake, and moved inland. It caused damage to a boat lift, boat, and several trees before dissipating just north of Airport Road.

An NWS Survey indicated a brief EF-0 tornado that moved across the City of Crystal, Minnesota. The tornado started near Memory Lane Park, between 43rd and 44th Avenue North and Jersey Avenue North. A large tree was uprooted at this location. This tornado moved eastward between 43rd and 44th Avenue and damaged several large trees, up to 4 feet in diameter, along its path. The tornado lifted near Douglas Drive North. Some roof damage occurred, but the majority of the trees and large limbs fell on power lines, roads, and yards. ||There was also damage on 45th Avenue North, but the damage was consistent with downburst winds and more sporadic. The majority of the damage in the broad area of New Hope, Crystal, North Minneapolis, and Robbinsdale was from downburst winds.

A shed's roof was blown off and an empty grain bin was blown over. The damage occurred 2 miles southwest of Waseca.

A trampoline was blown across the yard, a large tree was blown down, and a steel patio pergola was completely collapsed northwest of Steele Center. A large tree was blown down near Hope, and a large Ham antenna was blown down, along with a large playset lifted out of the ground between Lemond, and Hope.
Spotters sent pictures of large hailstones. The hailstones were described as at least half dollar size. The hailstones could have been larger based on the picture.

A trained spotter took video of a brief tornado that touched down in a wooded area and knocked down large branches.  Another spotter was also monitoring the storm. The tornado was also caught on video by a MNDOT camera along I-35 near Clinton Falls, so the timing could be confirmed. A broader view of the storm suggested this tornado had some characteristics similar to that of a satellite tornado just east of a larger tornado.

Trained spotters took video of a tornado that touched down in an open field and moved northward. It struck a farmstead at the end of its path, with only large branches knocked down per a NWS damage survey.

A brief touchdown was reported east-northeast of Henderson as it crossed Highway 19, moving from Le Sueur County into Scott County. It blew a trampoline and damaged a play set on the Le Sueur County side before moving north and damaging some trees in a grove  in Scott County per a NWS damage survey.
Two storm chasers took video of a narrow tornado.  A damage survey revealed that several trees were broken or blown down. Law enforcement and spotters were also watching the tornado.

A storm chaser took video of a tornado moving in an open field and then along a line of trees. Some of the trees were uprooted and lofted a couple hundred feet in the air. A NWS damage survey also noted uprooted trees.
Damage to a local farm was significant as a downburst likely caused an iron fence and a barn door to be blown down. There was also damage to trees and other farming structures.

Numerous videos, including some from trained spotters, showed a funnel cloud west of Owatonna. Toward the end, it became rope-like and then dissipated. None of the videos were close-up, and no debris cloud was ever noted, so ground contact contact could not be confirmed by video.  Two surveys by local officials and the NWS revealed no damage anywhere. Therefore this has been recorded as a funnel cloud. Videos showed another funnel cloud close to this one, and a separate entry has been made for that funnel.

Numerous videos, including some from trained spotters and a MNDOT traffic camera, showed a funnel cloud west of Owatonna. None of the videos were close-up, and no debris cloud was ever noted, so ground contact contact could not be confirmed by video.  Two surveys by local officials and the NWS revealed no damage anywhere. Therefore this has been recorded as a funnel cloud. Videos showed another funnel cloud (that was rope-like) close to this one, and a separate entry has been made for that funnel.

A storm chaser took video of a brief funnel cloud. It might have made ground contact but it was not possible to tell from the video, nor was there any damage noted. Therefore this has been recorded as a funnel cloud.

About one dozen homes were damaged, mostly due to some shingles, soffits or siding being torn off.  One house, however, had windows blown in and had partial roof damage.  It also had a garage that was completely blown apart and destroyed, but the garage had been added on and was not part of the original house itself. Another house had damage to its front porch overhang, which allowed wind to enter the attic and punch a hole through the roof on the backside of the house. At a farm, an old barn collapsed. At another house, part of the roof was blown off a machine shed.

Numerous trees were uprooted around the city of Sauk Centre.

There was a brief tornado just southeast of the intersection of Kandiyohi, Pope, and Stearns Counties. It was caught on video and moved across a bean field and road. Although it did not hit any damage indicators, video suggests the tornado was weak.

Several storm chasers documented a tornado that started in Belgrade. It knocked over several trees and numerous large branches in town, and took a few shingles and some soffit off a house. It then moved north-northeast out of town, across open fields, and dissipated.
There was a social media picture of half dollar size hail in Mankato.
There was a social media picture of golf ball size hail in the western portion of Mankato.

Several large trees, and powerlines were blown down in Glenwood, some were blocking roads. South of Kensington, several larger tree branches were blown down. Other areas along highway 55 had some tree branches blown down.  Trees and powerlines also blown down on the east side of Grove Lake, with two reported pontoons flipped over on Lake Minnewaska.
Severe winds damaged a local farm's roof and several trees were uprooted southwest of Padua.

Damage occurred north of Sacred Heart, and south of County Road 11. There was a metal roof that was blown several feet from its foundation and had its roof peeled off. Plus, several large trees were blown down. In addition, the farm had some of their corn flattened.
Several large tree branches were blown down south of St. Cloud, near Luxemburg.
A large tree was blown down on Highway 7, west of Hutchinson.
A couple of storms merged near Mahtomedi and intensified. This caused a dozen trees to be blown down around Mahtomedi.
A measured rainfall amount of 1.52 inches occurred with this storm.
A measured rainfall amount of 1.63 inches occurred with this storm.
A measured rainfall amount of 2.82 inches occurred with this storm.
A few large tree branches and a power line were blown down in the city of Appleton.
A large tree blew down along Highway 12, or 4 miles north of Appleton. The tree damage was posted on social media.
Several large tree branches blew down around the city of Glencoe. One of the branches was 10 inches in diameter and landed on a house.
A 55 knot wind gust was measured by a local storm spotter in Shakopee by a handheld wind sensor.

A few large trees were blown down in Shakopee, most of them rotted. The top wind speed recorded around Shakopee was 41 mph at the Jackson Township Mesonet site, located on Zumbro Ave., just south of Shakopee at about 1 PM CST.  Another spotter recorded a wind gust of 52 mph at her home in Savage.
A large tree was uprooted in Richfield.
There was a social media picture of a large tree that was snapped near the Chanhassen library.
Several trees were blown down in a golf course northeast of Waseca. These strong winds were associated with an outflow boundary from previous decaying thunderstorms.
A 62 mph wind gust was measured at the Owatonna airport and was associated with an outflow boundary from previous decaying thunderstorms.

Some lake homes were damaged along Silver Lake. On the western edge of the lake there was significant tree and dock damage. One boat was lofted 20 feet from the lake and landed between two large trees.
There was a barn and garage that was damaged, with corn flattened at County Road E and 160th Street.

A NWS Storm Survey determined that a downburst blew down hundreds of trees along a broad swath from 4 miles SSW of Deer Park, to 9 miles north of Baldwin. The trees were blown down from the north, northeast or east. There was roof damage to one local business.
A barn was destroyed south of Roberts.
Lightning struck two construction workers. One died and the other was transported to a local hospital with serious injuries.
There were multiple vehicles damaged with windows broken. In addition, siding on houses was damaged and numerous windows were broken to houses and outbuildings in and around Popple Creek.
Hail damaged siding in Sauk Rapids.
A trained spotter had a hand held wind sensor that measured the wind gust.
There were numerous reports of large tree branches blown down. There was also damage to MNDOT road signs and damage to cornfields.
There were numerous trees blown down in the town of Sauk Centre.
There were large trees blown down in Avon.
There were numerous large trees blown down along Highway 29, and along Lake Reno.
Several large trees and power lines were blown down near Upsala.
A few large trees were blown down north of Milaca.
A few trees were blown down, one large pine tree had its top blown off to the south near Isle.

There were several trees and many large branches blown down in the south half of Sleepy Eye, just east if Highway 4. A few trees and branches fell on houses and vehicles. A damage survey by the NWS was inconclusive, as the damage had been cleaned up quickly. The south to north path did seem to broaden out somewhat.
There were several trees blown down around the Sveadahl community.
A few trees were blown down in St. James.
A trained spotter had a hand held wind sensor that measured 52 knots.
A large tree was uprooted in Comfrey.
A large tree was snapped off the top, with several other smaller trees blown down north of Comfrey.
A large tree was broken off several feet above its base in Courtland.

Thousands of acres of corn were flattened by intense west and northwest winds across a broad area in western and southern Brown County. Some trees were blown down or damaged as well, including at a park on the northeast side of Altermatt Lake.
There were a number of large tree limbs blown down near Le Sueur. One that was 12 inches in diameter.
A trained spotter observed a funnel cloud north of Madelia.
A 12 inch diameter tree was snapped at its base north of Waconia.
A few trees were blown over, along with approximately 20 feet of corn flattened on the north side of Lake Tetonka.

Lightning struck a moviegoer at an east metro drive-in theater as storms moved through the area. The man was struck about 10:25 p.m CDT, Thursday, August, 5th at the Vali-Hi Drive-In just north of Interstate 94 in Lake Elmo.

Radar shows this tornado occurred with a flanking line, just south of precipitation echoes. A damage survey revealed mostly corn damage, but some large branches were knocked down at a farmstead and some plywood was blown into a field. The damage survey revealed it was tornadic.  Satellite imagery revealed more detail about the exact path through fields. Storm chaser video definitely shows the tornado and correct time, which was consistent with this being a tornado from a flanking line.

A storm chaser reported a brief tornado, and so a storm survey was conducted. The tornado tracked mostly across fields, but it did damage about two dozen trees, some of which were knocked over. The tornado was not always strong enough to produce corn and tree damage, but it did so occasionally along its path. The storm chaser took drone video a few days later, also revealing the tornado path.

Several trees and large branches were broken. A few hundred acres of corn were flattened at County Road 20 and 130th Avenue. An adjacent short damage path was determined to have been associated with a misocyclone, based on the damage pattern, Sentinel satellite imagery, and radar. It was not possible to correlate the crop damage with any radar circulation.
A funnel cloud was observed from the spotters northeast location along County Road 47.
Most of the hail was less than one inch in diameter.
There was a social media picture of the 2 diameter hail.
Radar suggested the hail size was much larger over Lake Mille Lacs, but there were no reports from that area.
A large tree fell on a power line.
A picture of 1 hail that fell north of Sacred Heart.

An EFO tornado tracked through a corn field and knocked down a few large branches in a grove of trees toward the end of the path. The path length was 1.6 miles with a width of 50 yards. Maximum wind speeds were 70 mph.

An EFO tornado touched down near Highway 13 and Connelly Parkway and moved east for 2.1 miles. There was sporadic damage along this path with maximum winds of 85 mph. Most of the damage was due to trees falling on houses and vehicles. The worst damage occurred near the intersection of Connelly Parkway and Dakota Avenue South where roof damage occurred at the Savage Public Works and Light. The city of Savage transformer station also had damage near this intersection, and most of the street lights and signs were damage.

An EF0 tornado touched down near the intersection of Highway 13, and Cliff Road in Burnsville. The path length was approximately 1 mile and most of the damage was due to trees falling on houses and vehicles.

An EF0 tornado touched down near Cedar Avenue and 145th Street West in Apple Valley. The path length was approximately 0.8 miles with a maximum wind speed of 80 mph. Most of the damage was due to trees falling on houses and vehicles.

A 64 mph wind gust was measured by the ASOS at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport. At MSP Airport, the force of the winds was so strong that two Boeing 737 airplanes belonging to Sun Country Airlines slid into each other and slammed into jet bridges, despite being secured with wheel chocks. There were reports of storm-related damage to other structures, vehicles, and equipment at the airport.
A private weather station measured a wind gust of 50 knots.
A private weather station measured a wind gust of 50 knots near Lydia.
A private weather sensor measured a wind gust of 50 knots southwest of Prior Lake.
Two large trees were blown down on Maple Street in St. Martin, and caused roof damage.
A few minor tree limbs blew down near Blaine and Columbia Heights as strong gusty winds moved across the county. One of the tree limbs landed on a power line, and another caused a fire.
This was a measured wind gust at the Benson airport. No other damage occurred around the area.
In the Industrial Park, on Spiral Blvd, there was a storage building leveled, and other assorted trees snapped. Most of the tree damage was on the south end of Hastings.
Sauk Centre airport reported a wind gust of 60 mph.
An area of significant downed trees was noted between Deer Creek, east-southeast toward Highway 65. The area is rural and not overly populated so damage was confined to cleanup on county roads.

Dunn County had reports of scattered minor damage across the county. There were a few areas that had more power outages related to downed trees and power lines. One area in the northwest portion of the county was between Connorsville and Boyceville.
This is the continuation of the minor damage across Dunn County. This area was more concentrated in southwest Dunn County between Weston and Eau Galle.

A large tree was blown down east of Ham Lake. Most wind sensors near the area only measured between 35 to 45 mph wind gusts, with the closest ASOS KANE (Anoka Airport) measuring between 15 to 25 mph during the time of the tree damage.
There were numerous downed power lines and large tree limbs around Chisago City, specifically along Old Towne Road.
A large tree was blown down in the city of New Ulm. The regional airport reported a wind gust of 61 mph as the storms moved through the city.
An outbuilding was blown down near Hanska. A couple wind sensors near the area had a peak wind gust of 45 mph near Hanska, and 53 mph near Madelia.
A semi-trailer flipped over on I-35 north of Highway 19. There was a wind gust of 58 mph near Elko New Market near the time of the incident.
Several tree branches were blown down between Cambridge and Isanti. Based on several wind sensors near the area, the highest wind gusts were around 40 mph.
Several trees were damaged or uprooted in Nicollet. The highest wind speeds around the area were between 45 and 55 mph.
A tree branch fell onto a tent at the Land of Memories Park. A family was in the tent and a 4 year old girl was killed from injuries of the fallen tree branch.
A large tree blew down in Bloomington.

Several trees were blown down or uprooted in Richfield. There was also significant tree damage in the Fort Snelling cemetery. At least 50 mature trees were damage or uprooted in the cemetery adjacent to the MSP airport.
A few tree branches were blown down.
A weather sensor had a wind gust of 58 mph near the intersection of Highway 13 and County Road 42. Several small tree limbs also blew down in the area.
Numerous trees were blown down between Lexington and Pilot Knob Road, and along Cliff Road in Eagan. A few of the trees landed on roofs and cars.
A few large trees were blown down in Rosemount.
A large tree was uprooted near I-35 and Nicollet Avenue in Burnsville.
A large tree branch was blown down in Lakeville.
Several trees were uprooted near I-35, south of the old Burnsville Center.
Multiple trees were uprooted or blown down near I-494 and I-35E in Eagan.

There were numerous downed trees and power lines in and around the city of Hudson. Significant damage occurred to the Hudson library. Windows were blown out and debris blew into the library and surrounding areas.

A large tree was snapped near its base, west of Roberts. Several smaller tree limbs were also blown down around the same area. This is the continuation of the strong winds that occurred in the Hudson area.

An isolated thunderstorm produced a lightning bolt that injured three  construction workers at the Minneapolis International Airport. All three were alert when rescue workers arrived. Two refused medical treatment and one person was taken to Hennepin County Medical Center with minor injuries. Information provided by Minneapolis Star Tribune newspaper.

A small and narrow misocyclone on the leading edge of a storm traveled across corn and bean fields only. Drone video was utilized and an on-site survey was performed. The path was also identified using Sentinel satellite imagery. It was not possible to correlate the crop damage with any radar circulation.
Satellite imagery revealed a damage path through crops, and a damage survey noted large branches down. Time based on radar. QLCS tornado.
One tree was snapped in half near Hastings.
Minor tree damage occurred west of the tornado near Highway 13, and County Road 42. in Savage.
A pole barn had its entire roof blown off the west side, and a couple panels on the east side. The metal, some rafter parts, and a lot of cellulose loose insulation were strewn all to the east.
There was a downed tree and a bent light post in Shakopee, west of St. Francis Hospital.
A few trees were blown down south of New Richmond. The trees looked hollow and weak. There was a private weather wind sensor near the area that reported a wind gust of 64 mph.
Satellite imagery revealed a damage path through crops, and a damage survey noted large branches down in two locations. Time based on radar. QLCS tornado.
Track based on satellite imagery and damage survey. Time based on radar. Tornado knocked down large branches in a small grove at the end of its path.
Satellite image showed tornado path through corn that matched up with circulation on radar. Damage survey could not locate any downed branches or any other damage indicator.

A damage survey noted several trees were damaged at a farmstead, with large branches down. Satellite imagery showed more details to the tornado path. A time-stamped photo from a storm chaser showed a visible funnel in the area where the tornado damage occurred, and the photo was consistent with the tornado being in the flanking line.

Mainly tree damage. Some trees fell on sheds, houses and vehicles. Two sheds had their roofs partially removed. Time estimated from radar.

This tornado first caused damage to groves of trees southwest of Stanley, then affected a couple farmsteads. It intensified significantly as it approached Stanley, demolishing an outbuilding and then two outbuildings with a construction business. An historic train depot had a portion of its roof removed. A high tension power line was blown down. About six homes had their roofs removed, and in the northeast edge of Stanley, a roof and outer walls were removed from a portion of a house. The tornado continued into northwestern Clark County where it damaged more trees and outbuildings (see entry from NWS La Crosse).

A strong arctic cold front moved into central and southern Minnesota on January 1, dropping temperatures below zero.  A two year old boy in New Ulm wandered into the cold sometime Wednesday morning, January 2, and was found by his mother at 0745 CST, less than one block from home. He was pronounced dead at the New Ulm Medical Center.  The temperature at New Ulm airport dropped below zero around 0100 CST, and fell to eight below zero by 0700 CST.  The temperature warmed back above zero by 1000 CST.

A barn lost its roof. Large tree limbs were also downed. This tornado began in Winnebago County, Iowa (see entry from NWS Des Moines).
A narrow path of mostly tree damage was found just to the west of SE 89th Ave. An irrigation system was overturned, some farm outbuildings were damaged, and a small shed was tossed.

A tornado spun up south of Kenyon around County 11 Blvd and 50th Ave and continued northeast. It destroyed a few farm outbuildings and snapped several trees near 480th street. Debris was lofted west across 66th Ave.

Tornado developed in Dodge County (see entry from NWS La Crosse). It spun up just south of the Goodhue/Dodge county border near 170th Ave and tracked northeast. It snapped pine trees, destroyed the top half of a barn, and lofted debris westward into a field. It ended around 100th Ave south of County 54 Blvd.

The first damage observed was a bent road sign near the tornado origin point. A path of tree and utility pole damage continued to the northeast before ending just south of I-90. Several trees were uprooted.

This tornado developed to the east of Alden, damaging trees and a large building that housed farm equipment. It then continued to the northeast, damaging additional trees before dissipating in a field.

A fast-moving tornado touched down to the southwest of Hartland and moved into town, damaging numerous buildings, trees, and utility poles. The damage in the southern residential part of town was mainly tree and roof damage. As the tornado tracked into the center of town, more significant damage was observed to buildings along Broadway Street. The most significant damage was to two buildings along Broadway and Johnson in the center of town with significant damage to the walls of low-rise commercial buildings. More tree and roof damage was observed to the northeast with some branches observed along State Highway 13. The tornado dissipated to the northeast in a field with no further damage observed.

This tornado hit several farms, including one where seven buildings had enough damage so they will be totaled. Several windows of a house were blown out. A machine shed at another farm had several pillars of a large machine shed pulled out of the ground. At the end of the tornado, a home had many shingles removed.

The tornado hit one farmstead, knocking down trees and causing some damage to outbuildings. At the next farmstead, it destroyed a machine shed. A nearly full grain bin was dented at the top. The house had part of its roof taken off. Near the end of its path, two irrigation pivots were blown over. It was uncertain whether the tornado moved into Mower County, and so the path was not extended into Mower County.

This tornado developed in Worth County Iowa along 500th Street, initially producing some tree damage (see separate entry from NWS Des Moines).  As it crossed into Freeborn County Minnesota, it displaced and destroyed an empty silo on State Line Road. It then destroyed a cattle barn and a pole crashed through a car. The tornado then continued to produce mostly minor tree damage and moved northeast into southwestern Mower County (see separate entry from NWS La Crosse).

A brief tornado occurred south of Glenville. It spun up around 782nd Ave and tracked northeast producing some tree damage until it reached 795th Ave. There, it damaged farm buildings and tossed hay bales across the road.
This tornado hit several farmsteads, partially removing the roofs of several outbuildings and a turkey barn. It dented a silo. Trees fell on a number of sheds and vehicles.
